Since the remainder is $0,$ it means that $x+1$ divides $5x^4+x^3+6x+2$ exactly and gives a quotient of $5x^3-4x^2+4x+2.$

So, we have

$$
\dfrac{5x^4+x^3+6x+2}{x+1} = 5x^3-4x^2+4x+2 .
$$"] [17592186083005 :question/problem "Find the quotient and remainder of $\dfrac{3x^4+7x^3-10x+8}{2-3x}.$"] [17592186083005 :question/worked-solution "First, we write the divisor in standard form as $-3x+2.$ Then, we factor out the leading coefficient. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{x}^{4}+7{x}^{3}-10x+8}{-3x+2} & =\frac{3{x}^{4}+7{x}^{3}-10x+8}{-3(x-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\frac{3{x}^{4}+7{x}^{3}-10x+8}{(x-\frac{2}{3})}).\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on $\dfrac{3x^4+7x^3-10x+8}{\left(x-\frac23\right)},$ remembering to include a coefficient of zero for the $x^2$ term, we arrive at the following:

![](images/7a/7a44598088833fa475191b39579bb82935074ae5c470e5a2139555818b91af08.svg)

Reading off the bottom row, we get

$$
\frac{3x^4+7x^3-10x+8}{\left(x-\frac23\right)} = 3x^3+9x^2+6x-6+\frac{4}{\left(x-\frac23\right)}.
$$

Finally, we multiply by the original $-\dfrac 1 3$ factor to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{x}^{4}+7{x}^{3}-10x+8}{2-3x} & =-\frac{1}{3}(3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+6x-6+\frac{4}{(x-\frac{2}{3})}) \\  & =-{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-2x+2+\frac{4}{2-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186083930 :question/problem "$\frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-4}{x-3}=$"] [17592186083930 :question/worked-solution "We can calculate $\frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-4}{x-3}$ using synthetic division.

Carrying out the synthetic division process, we arrive at the following:

|  | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $3$ | $2$ | $-3$ | $-4$ |
|  | $↓$ | $6$ | $9$ |
|  | $2$ | $3$ | $5$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-4}{x-3}=2x+3+\frac{5}{x-3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186083930 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-a089de6a-9ae9-59ae-bc4b-65be3819ab12" :answer/id #uuid "a089de6a-9ae9-59ae-bc4b-65be3819ab12"] "$\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2x+1}=$"] ["question-74edae7f-921c-52ab-b265-0f5c05fcd5a7" :question/worked-solution "We can calculate $\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2x+1}$ using synthetic division.

For synthetic division to work, we need the coefficient of $x$ in the denominator to be equal to $1.$ So first, we factor the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2x+1} & =\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2(x+\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on $\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}$, we arrive at the following:

$$

$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on $\frac{18{x}^{2}+27x}{(x-\frac{1}{6})}$, we arrive at the following:

|  | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |

| $\frac{1}{6}$ | $18$ | $27$ | $0$ |
|  | $↓$ | $3$ | $5$ |

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{18{x}^{2}+27x}{(x-\frac{1}{6})} & =\frac{1}{6}(18x+30+\frac{5}{(x-\frac{1}{6})}) \\  & =3x+5+\frac{5}{6x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=8\,\text{cm},$ $C=2\pi (8)=16\pi \text{ cm}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-32\pi $ and $C=16\pi ,$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-32\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{16\pi }{2\pi } \\ -32\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot 8 \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}"] ["question-7842bd80-84fe-5d31-bbd1-38dac51d5756" :question/worked-solution "Let $r$ be the radius of the hailstone, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =12\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & =(12\sqrt{\pi })^{2} \\ A & =144\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =144\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =36 \\ r & =6.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7842bd80-84fe-5d31-bbd1-38dac51d5756" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-e74b5676-bbc7-5018-8226-6434bdbb2081" :answer-field/id #uuid is $(-5,4)$ and leading coefficient is $2.$"] ["question-39734cdd-98b1-5bc5-a3ba-0e209592784a" :question/worked-solution "Remember that the vertex form of a parabola is

$$
y=a(x-h)^{2}+k,
$$

where $(h,k)$ are the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola, and $a$ is the leading coefficient.

Substituting $(h,k)=(-5,4)$ and $a=2$ into the above and then expanding and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(x-(-5))^{2}+4 \\  & =2(x+5)^{2}+4 \\  & =2({x}^{2}+10x+25)+4 \\  & =2{x}^{2}+20x+50+4 \\  & =2{x}^{2}+20x+54.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is $y=2{x}^{2}+20x+54.$"] ["question-39734cdd-98b1-5bc5-a3ba-0e209592784a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $y=-2{x}^{2}-8x-14$ in vertex form."] ["question-1b44bc96-863e-5a73-a2ed-628d5188e295" :question/worked-solution "To express the equation of the parabola in vertex form, we need to complete the square. 

First, we take out a factor of $-2$ from the entire expression:

$$
-2{x}^{2}-8x-14=-2({x}^{2}+4x+7)
$$

Now, we complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x+7 & = \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot x+7 & = \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+7 & = \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2})-{2}^{2}+7 & = \\ (x+2)^{2}-{2}^{2}+7 & = \\ (x+2)^{2}-4+7 & = \\ (x+2)^{2}+3 & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2({x}^{2}+4x+7) & = \\ -2((x+2)^{2}+3) & = \\ -2(x+2)^{2}-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, expressed in vertex form, the equation of the parabola is $y=-2(x+2)^{2}-6.$"] ["question-1b44bc96-863e-5a73-a2ed-628d5188e295" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] tells us that if $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix with full rank (i.e., $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$), then there exists a unique inverse matrix $A^{-1}$ such that 

$$
AA^{-1}=A^{-1}\!A=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ denotes the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

There are two questions that we can ask:

- Can we extend the notion of an inverse matrix to one that works for $n\times n$ matrices $A$ where $\mathrm{rank}(A) < n?$

- Is it possible to generalize the concept of an inverse to non-square matrices?

The answer to both questions is yes! This generalization of the inverse of $A$ is called the **pseudoinverse** of $A,$ and is denoted $A^+.$ The dimensions of $A^+$ are the same as $A^T.$

As an example, let's consider the ${\color{red}{3}}\times {\color{blue}{2}}$ matrix $A$ and its corresponding pseudoinverse, given below:

![](images/87/87581a69d3d76dbf3b0ebca8941c9a82b5b9443b00e86f32e4e9e4a42ef5e18b.svg)

- Computing $A^{+}\!A,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+}\,A & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which is the identity matrix $I_{\color{blue}{2}}.$

- Computing $A\!A^{+},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{+} & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is *almost* the identity matrix $I_{\color{red}{3}}.$

We can explain this result using the following properties of the pseudoinverse:

- *If the columns of an $m\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $A^+A = I_{\color{blue}{n}}.$*

- *If the rows of an ${\color{red}{m}}\times n$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $AA^+ = I_{\color{red}{m}}.$*

In the example above, the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, but the rows are not.

Moreover, the notion of a pseudoinverse is consistent with inverse matrices. In particular,

*If $A$ is an invertible square matrix, then $A^{+} = A^{-1}.$*

This lesson will discuss how to compute the pseudoinverse for any matrix, starting with an important special case."] [17592186163314 :tutorial/content "For an *almost* zero ${\color{red}{m}}\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix with non-zero entries

$$

$$

on the main diagonal only.

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0.64 \\ \operatorname{arccos}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(0.64) \\ \theta  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(0.64)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\alpha  & =1.25 \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\alpha ) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1.25) \\ \alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1.25).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using a calculator, we find

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=50\,\text{km/h}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+y}{6.25} & =\frac{y}{3.75} \\ 3.75x+3.75y & =6.25y \\ 3.75x & =2.5y \\ y & =1.5x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =1.5\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=50\,\text{km/h}$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =75\,\text{km/h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the bus' shadow increases at $75\,\text{km/h}.$"] ["question-28170d6f-d1bf-54a6-9dab-69ada5f8b07e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$

Finally, substituting $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4.5\,\text{m/s}$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{7}{18}\cdot (4.5) \\  & =1.75\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the velocity of the cat's shadow is *negative* because the cat is walking *toward* Harry, and therefore the distance between Harry and the cat *decreases* with time.

Since we want to calculate $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we need to find a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Since the two triangles are similar, the ratios between the corresponding sides are equal, and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+y}{30} & =\frac{y}{10} \\ 10x+10y & =30y \\ 10x & =20y \\ x & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate both sides of the above equation with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2y) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=-11\,\text{in/s}$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2(-11)=-22\,\text{in/s}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the speed of the cat is $22\,\text{in/s}.$"] ["question-21055998-26d2-5a03-b3c0-e38582a8d839" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ![](images/0a/0a47e801db651c027415a7943e5327bd378c1a08e533dc69673ab4304c8cc7b4.png)

In the figure, $x$ is the actor’s distance from the wall, while $y$ is the length of the shadow. Both $x$ and $y$ change with time. In particular, we know that the actor’s velocity is

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3\,\text{ft/s}.
$$

Notice that the actor’s velocity is *negative* because it is moving *toward* the wall, and therefore the distance between it and the wall *decreases* with time.

Since we want to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we need to find a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Since the two triangles are similar, the ratios between the corresponding sides are equal, and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{(18-x)+x} & =\frac{6}{18-x} \\ \frac{y}{18} & =\frac{6}{18-x} \\ y & =\frac{108}{18-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate both sides with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{108}{18-x}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{108}{(18-x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=18-8=10\,\text{ft}$ and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3\,\text{ft/s}$ into the above expression gives, to one decimal place

$$

Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le 2+x-y\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/65/65c61ad7dc2964cd0de9a6bbdf259fcf3388e25da4eaabf155d58ff0c05c8d55.png)

Hence, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 2+x-y\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+x-y}dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[z]_{z=0}^{z=2+x-y}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2+x-y)-0\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}2+x-y\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[(2+x)y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2+x-\frac{1}{2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{2}+x\,dx \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(3+2)-0 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1f0b5299-7a35-5c1a-9b72-d6af14bd952f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bb4d67ee-c5f9-5907-9389-cb8d07771ac8" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}+3x-2
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x-2
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{3}{2})}^{2},$ writing the constant term $2$ last:

$$
{{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-2
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-2
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{17}{4}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2({x}^{2}+3x-2) & =-2({(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{17}{4}) \\  & =-2{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+(-2)\cdot (-\frac{17}{4}) \\  & =-2{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+\frac{17}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-db65568c-c0a4-5de2-8240-a716b187636f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-ece1c1a9-e6aa-5e0f-8f5d-a9fac0d03848" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}z+2
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{1}{2})}^{2},$ writing the constant term $2$ last:

$$
{{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}z+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+2
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+2
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{7}{4}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-({z}^{2}+z+2) & =-({(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{7}{4}) \\  & =-{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8c5fa084-327e-5d66-96c0-960c479aa7b9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-90dc3305-1623-5c23-9c54-7ae3dcbc7551" :answer-field/id #uuid where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨0,\,0,\,-2y⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=4-x-2y.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above."] [17592186134130 :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=4-x-2y.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=4-x-2y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-x-2y)=-1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-x-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨0,\,0,\,-2y⟩{|}_{z=4-x-2y} \\  & =⟨{{0}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2y}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-1)-0\cdot (-2)+(-2y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-palne is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2r\cdot r\,\text{d}r \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot [{r}^{2}]_{r=0}^{r=1} \\  & =(1-1)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186134130 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-7903ed28-5d25-5da8-85e5-0a207c57c64f" :answer/id #uuid "7903ed28-5d25-5da8-85e5-0a207c57c64f"] ["question-19360ab0-63c4-5cd8-9a4a-b29910944cd3" :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=x\,i-z\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\,i+({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,j+k$ for $t\in [0,1).$"] ["question-19360ab0-63c4-5cd8-9a4a-b29910944cd3" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2},\,z=1.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i-z\,k \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)\,i-1\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-2t)\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{2}-t)\,i-\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-2t)\,j) \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (3{t}^{2}-2t)+(-1)\cdot 0 \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}-t)(2t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{({t}^{2}-t)^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-19360ab0-63c4-5cd8-9a4a-b29910944cd3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-81425c09-b875-5245-8a44-a234fc04ecfd" :answer-field/id #uuid If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{2}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (2x)-x\cdot (-2y)+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,2\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-22c4166d-7812-5cc0-89d7-bc30157982f0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-bce8cadb-6f17-5458-a146-66e868571308" :answer-field/id #uuid "bce8cadb-6f17-5458-a146-66e868571308"] ["answer-580a54b0-7193-5059-b069-221fd5506992" :answer/id #uuid "580a54b0-7193-5059-b069-221fd5506992"] ["answer-580a54b0-7193-5059-b069-221fd5506992" :answer/type :answer.type/text] ["answer-580a54b0-7193-5059-b069-221fd5506992" :answer/value "$$

If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+y\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-0\cdot \pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186134134 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-6eea3a9c-148b-5bbc-b698-c42d3d976666" :answer/id #uuid "6eea3a9c-148b-5bbc-b698-c42d3d976666"] ["answer-6eea3a9c-148b-5bbc-b698-c42d3d976666" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-6eea3a9c-148b-5bbc-b698-c42d3d976666" :answer/value "-2\pi "] ["answer-9ce79bec-631d-5e6e-9ada-b94ec4a0d8f0" :answer/id #uuid "9ce79bec-631d-5e6e-9ada-b94ec4a0d8f0"] ["answer-9ce79bec-631d-5e6e-9ada-b94ec4a0d8f0" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-9ce79bec-631d-5e6e-9ada-b94ec4a0d8f0" :answer/value "2\pi "] ["answer-81f2f5fe-c2fa-5a14-a755-d561c640ccb1" :answer/id #uuid "81f2f5fe-c2fa-5a14-a755-d561c640ccb1"] ["answer-81f2f5fe-c2fa-5a14-a755-d561c640ccb1" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-81f2f5fe-c2fa-5a14-a755-d561c640ccb1" :answer/value "\pi "] [17592186130960 :answer-field/correct "answer-81f2f5fe-c2fa-5a14-a755-d561c640ccb1"] [17592186130960 :answer-field/choices "answer-6eea3a9c-148b-5bbc-b698-c42d3d976666"] [17592186130960 :answer-field/choices "answer-9ce79bec-631d-5e6e-9ada-b94ec4a0d8f0"] [17592186130960 :answer-field/choices "answer-81f2f5fe-c2fa-5a14-a755-d561c640ccb1"] ["question-2bdcc65b-8401-5044-8aa5-c9a7e37ffa6b" :question/id #uuid "2bdcc65b-8401-5044-8aa5-c9a7e37ffa6b"] ["question-2bdcc65b-8401-5044-8aa5-c9a7e37ffa6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-162890"] ["question-2bdcc65b-8401-5044-8aa5-c9a7e37ffa6b" :question/problem "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=2z\,i+x\,j+3y\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$"] ["question-2bdcc65b-8401-5044-8aa5-c9a7e37ffa6b" :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2z\,i+x\,j+3y\,k \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t-12{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2{cos}^{2}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t-14{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-14{sin}^{2}⁡t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-14{sin}^{2}⁡t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-7(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-5+7\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-5t+\frac{7}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(1-5(2\pi )+0)-(1-5(0)+0) \\  & =-10\pi \end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2bdcc65b-8401-5044-8aa5-c9a7e37ffa6b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-fd517342-4196-5078-a01c-54f228cf9d0a" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-9b89dfe3-da21-530c-903d-947ec6af3854"] [17592186074263 :question/problem "$\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=$"] [17592186074263 :question/worked-solution "First, we convert $\frac{\pi }{4}$ radians to an equivalent measure in degrees. This gives

$$
(\frac{\pi }{4})(\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi })=\frac{{180}^{∘}}{4}={45}^{∘}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=\operatorname{tan}⁡{45}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, since we know that $\operatorname{tan}⁡{45}^{∘}=1,$ we obtain

- Statement I is true. Converting ${15}^{∘}$ from degrees to radians, we get

$$
{15}^{∘}=15\cdot \frac{\pi }{180}=\frac{\pi }{12}\,\text{radians}.
$$

- Statement II is false. Converting ${20}^{∘}$ from degrees to radians, we get

$$
{20}^{∘}=20\cdot \frac{\pi }{180}=\frac{\pi }{9}\,\text{radians}.
$$

The statement is false because $\frac{\pi }{9}\ne \frac{5\pi }{36}.$

- Statement III is true. Converting ${35}^{∘}$ from degrees to radians, we get 

$$
{35}^{∘}=35\cdot \frac{\pi }{180}=\frac{7\pi }{36}\,\text{radians}.
$$

So, the correct answer is 'I and III only'."] ["question-5168a992-4557-5020-911a-67c9df9985ed" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-1af2aa0f-c2a3-543f-a83e-691c13f6818c" $$

$$

1[P]=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}

["question-e022df96-ab83-5f54-81a6-300069e7bfc3" :question/math-academy-id "q-346680"] ["question-e022df96-ab83-5f54-81a6-300069e7bfc3" :question/problem "Consider the function

$$
f(x)=1[x\ge -1]\cdot {x}^{2}+1[x<-1]\cdot (-x).
$$

What is $f(-3)?$"] ["question-e022df96-ab83-5f54-81a6-300069e7bfc3" :question/worked-solution "The indicator function $1[P]$ equals $1$ if the predicate $P$ is true and $0$ if $P$ is false.

$$
1[P]=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-3,$ we evaluate each indicator function:

- $1[x\ge -1]=1[-3\ge -1]=0$ (since $-3\ge -1$ is false)

- $1[x<-1]=1[-3<-1]=1$ (since $-3<-1$ is true)

Substituting into the expression for $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-3) & =1[-3\ge -1]\cdot (-3)^{2}+1[-3<-1]\cdot (-(-3)) \\  & =0\cdot 9+1\cdot 3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the indicator functions act as a "switch": since $x=-3<-1,$ the first term vanishes and only the second term contributes to the result."] ["question-e022df96-ab83-5f54-81a6-300069e7bfc3" {x}_{1}=-3,\,{x}_{2}=6,\,{x}_{3}=0,\,{x}_{4}=2,\,{x}_{5}=-1
$$

Given the values ${x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4},\,{x}_{5}$ above, we have

${\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i}=$ {{field-1}}."] ["question-ce2c0db9-ad0b-5196-91d2-2f4a888aa062" :question/worked-solution "The indicator function $1[P]$ equals $1$ if the predicate $P$ is true and $0$ if $P$ is false.

$$
1[P]=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression $1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i}$ equals ${x}_{i}$ when ${x}_{i}>0$ and equals $0$ otherwise. Thus, the sum 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i}
$$

adds up only the positive values.

We evaluate the indicator function for each ${x}_{i}:$

- $1[{x}_{1}>0]=1[-3>0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{2}>0]=1[6>0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{3}>0]=1[0>0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{4}>0]=1[2>0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{5}>0]=1[-1>0]=0$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i} & =0\cdot (-3)+1\cdot 6+0\cdot 0+1\cdot 2+0\cdot (-1) \\  & =0+6+0+2+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ce2c0db9-ad0b-5196-91d2-2f4a888aa062" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-51fa0505-47ca-5c35-ba62-02fa3db61539" :answer-field/id #uuid "51fa0505-47ca-5c35-ba62-02fa3db61539"] ["answer-80a200ec-9e32-5842-a3a1-191293b65d99" :answer/id #uuid "80a200ec-9e32-5842-a3a1-191293b65d99"] ["answer-80a200ec-9e32-5842-a3a1-191293b65d99" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-80a200ec-9e32-5842-a3a1-191293b65d99" :answer/value "8"] ["answer-field-51fa0505-47ca-5c35-ba62-02fa3db61539" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-51fa0505-47ca-5c35-ba62-02fa3db61539" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-51fa0505-47ca-5c35-ba62-02fa3db61539" :answer-field/correct "answer-80a200ec-9e32-5842-a3a1-191293b65d99"] ["answer-field-51fa0505-47ca-5c35-ba62-02fa3db61539" :answer-field/choices "answer-80a200ec-9e32-5842-a3a1-191293b65d99"] ["question-ce2c0db9-ad0b-5196-91d2-2f4a888aa062" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-51fa0505-47ca-5c35-ba62-02fa3db61539"] [17592186166969 :knowledge-point/questions "question-ce2c0db9-ad0b-5196-91d2-2f4a888aa062"] ["question-f9506abb-49a9-5357-8f1d-b8154670131b" :question/id #uuid "f9506abb-49a9-5357-8f1d-b8154670131b"] ["question-f9506abb-49a9-5357-8f1d-b8154670131b" :question/math-academy-id "q-346673"] ["question-f9506abb-49a9-5357-8f1d-b8154670131b" :question/problem "$$

Given the values ${x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4},\,{x}_{5}$ above, we have

${\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot ({x}_{i}-1)+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 2=$ {{field-1}}."] ["question-7ce60c02-eb25-536f-a376-c9d5685f21ea" :question/worked-solution "The indicator function $1[P]$ equals $1$ if the predicate $P$ is true and $0$ if $P$ is false.

$$
1[P]=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression $1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot ({x}_{i}-1)+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 2$ equals ${x}_{i}-1$ when ${x}_{i}\ge 0$ and equals $2$ when ${x}_{i}<0.$ Thus, the sum

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot ({x}_{i}-1)+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 2
$$

adds ${x}_{i}-1$ for nonnegative values and $2$ for negative values.

We evaluate the indicator function for each ${x}_{i}:$

- $1[{x}_{1}\ge 0]=1[-3\ge 0]=0,$ $1[{x}_{1}<0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{2}\ge 0]=1[1\ge 0]=1,$ $1[{x}_{2}<0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{3}\ge 0]=1[6\ge 0]=1,$ $1[{x}_{3}<0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{4}\ge 0]=1[-2\ge 0]=0,$ $1[{x}_{4}<0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{5}\ge 0]=1[0\ge 0]=1,$ $1[{x}_{5}<0]=0$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot ({x}_{i}-1)+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 2 & =2+(1-1)+(6-1)+2+(0-1) \\  & =2+0+5+2-1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7ce60c02-eb25-536f-a376-c9d5685f21ea" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8470a13f-71f6-57ad-8421-53498bc36c05" :answer-field/id #uuid "8470a13f-71f6-57ad-8421-53498bc36c05"] ["answer-50fd8bc5-cefc-5845-bbed-5233a3393494" :answer/id #uuid "50fd8bc5-cefc-5845-bbed-5233a3393494"] ["answer-50fd8bc5-cefc-5845-bbed-5233a3393494" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-50fd8bc5-cefc-5845-bbed-5233a3393494" :answer/value "8"] ["answer-field-8470a13f-71f6-57ad-8421-53498bc36c05" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-8470a13f-71f6-57ad-8421-53498bc36c05" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-8470a13f-71f6-57ad-8421-53498bc36c05" :answer-field/correct "answer-50fd8bc5-cefc-5845-bbed-5233a3393494"] ["answer-field-8470a13f-71f6-57ad-8421-53498bc36c05" :answer-field/choices "answer-50fd8bc5-cefc-5845-bbed-5233a3393494"] ["question-7ce60c02-eb25-536f-a376-c9d5685f21ea" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-8470a13f-71f6-57ad-8421-53498bc36c05"] [17592186166969 :knowledge-point/questions "question-7ce60c02-eb25-536f-a376-c9d5685f21ea"] ["question-cde00f71-de2d-5ff7-ae71-1ddcfa0a1b1f" :question/id #uuid "cde00f71-de2d-5ff7-ae71-1ddcfa0a1b1f"] ["question-cde00f71-de2d-5ff7-ae71-1ddcfa0a1b1f" :question/math-academy-id "q-347433"] ["question-cde00f71-de2d-5ff7-ae71-1ddcfa0a1b1f" :question/problem "Consider the function

$$

For $x=-3,$ we evaluate each indicator function:

- $1[x\ge 2]=1[-3\ge 2]=0$ (since $-3\ge 2$ is false)

- $1[-1\le x<2]=1[-1\le -3<2]=0$ (since $-1\le -3$ is false)

- $1[x<-1]=1[-3<-1]=1$ (since $-3<-1$ is true)

Substituting into the expression for $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-3) & =1[-3\ge 2]\cdot (-5)^{2}+1[-1\le -3<2]\cdot 1+1[-3<-1]\cdot (-(-3)) \\  & =0\cdot 25+0\cdot 1+1\cdot 3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

indicator function $\mathbf{1}_A(x)$ of a set $A$ equals $1$ if $x \in A$ and $0$ if $x \notin A.$ 
![](images/c1/c12d2f59eb7eb9730fc7576bb426cff90a3cff4ac8577c3f212db8101197300b.svg)

In this lesson, we introduce a more general notation that allows us to write indicator functions for any condition, not just set membership.

The **Iverson bracket notation** $\mathbf{1}[P]$ takes a predicate $P$ and returns
![](images/4d/4dbe29e205fecf97bd7d4c0bfbf810c7336a6a50198fa35319e7ae8b0ac505c0.svg)

For example:

- $\mathbf{1}[3 > 2] = 1$ because $3 > 2$ is true.

- $\mathbf{1}[5 \leq 4] = 0$ because $5 \leq 4$ is false.

- $\mathbf{1}[7 \in \{2, 5, 7\}] = 1$ because $7$ is an element of $\{2, 5, 7\}.$"] [17592186168059 :tutorial/content "The set-based notation from the previous lesson is a special case of Iverson bracket notation. Specifically,

$$
\mathbf{1}_A(x) = \mathbf{1}[x \in A].
$$

Both expressions equal $1$ when $x \in A$ and $0$ when $x \notin A.$ 

The Iverson bracket is more flexible because it works with any predicate, such as inequalities. For example:
![](images/cd/cd01819adb510c2b439f44089b1bd3cbd1f49e671779039fdf2f6be62a39810f.svg)"] [17592186168051 :tutorial/content "Indicator functions are useful for writing expressions that behave differently depending on whether a condition is met.

**Sums with indicator functions.** When we multiply a term by an indicator function inside a sum, the indicator acts as a filter. For example, given values $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n,$ the sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}[x_i > 0] \cdot x_i
$$

adds up only the positive values. If $x_i > 0,$ the indicator equals $1$ and the term contributes $x_i.$ If $x_i \leq 0,$ the indicator equals $0$ and the term contributes nothing.

Consider the values $x_1 = 5, x_2 = -3, x_3 = 2.$ Using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i} & =1[5>0]\cdot 5+1[-3>0]\cdot (-3)+1[2>0]\cdot 2 \\  & =1\cdot 5+0\cdot (-3)+1\cdot 2 \\  & =5+0+2 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}[x_i > 0]$ counts the positive values. For this data, the count is $1 + 0 + 1 = 2.$"] [17592186168060 :tutorial/content "Indicator functions can also express piecewise functions compactly. Consider the absolute value function:
![](images/33/336dc8080661db77e7ac701204aa6a32075bc7f4bd06625f4e8467e87a5c075c.svg)

We can write this as a single expression using indicator functions:

$$
|x| = \mathbf{1}[x \geq 0] \cdot x + \mathbf{1}[x < 0] \cdot (-x).
$$

Since the conditions $x \geq 0$ and $x < 0$ are mutually exclusive, exactly one indicator equals $1$ and the other equals $0.$ This "switch" mechanism selects the appropriate term automatically.

Let's verify this expression for a negative number, say $x = -4{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|-4| & =1[-4\ge 0]\cdot (-4)+1[-4<0]\cdot (-(-4)) \\  & =0\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 4 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186167001 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-d82dc916-4a3b-544e-8c9e-9820eeb6151d" :question/id #uuid "d82dc916-4a3b-544e-8c9e-9820eeb6151d"] ["question-d82dc916-4a3b-544e-8c9e-9820eeb6151d" :question/math-academy-id "q-100057"] ["question-d82dc916-4a3b-544e-8c9e-9820eeb6151d" :question/problem "![](images/6d/6dd62794ee072530cd2b6c8028101b58ae617d6757d29f79de90d1a439f6529b.png)

the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2u+v) \\ uv\end{aligned}].$"] [17592186129634 :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2u+v)$ and $y=uv.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{2}{2u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{2u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{2u+v} & \frac{1}{2u+v} \\ \,\text{ }v\, & \,\text{ }u\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{2}{2u+v}\cdot u-\frac{1}{2u+v}\cdot v \\  & =\frac{2u-v}{2u+v}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186129634 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-b6ea50ce-74b8-5b02-885a-93867c7a6416" :answer/id #uuid "b6ea50ce-74b8-5b02-885a-93867c7a6416"] The sides of a square are increasing in length at a rate of $3\text{ mm/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the square changing when the sides have a length of $12\text{ mm}?$"] [17592186064640 :question/worked-solution "Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is increasing at a rate of $3\,\text{mm/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3.$ Also, when the sides are $12\,\text{mm},$ we have $x=12.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =3\cdot 2(12)=72{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(6)\cdot 2(4)=48{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

The relationship between $p$ and $h$ is

$$
p=2\sqrt{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each diagonal of the square is increasing at a rate of $4\sqrt{2}\text{ feet}\text{/hour},$ so we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=4\sqrt{2}.
$$

Substituting this information into the above expression for $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =(4\sqrt{2})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=16\text{ feet/hour}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the perimeter of the square increases at $16\text{ feet}/\text{hour}.$"] ["question-5082ae1f-b15c-594a-83e6-841946d45040" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] The diagonals of a square increase in length at a rate of $1.5\text{ mm/min}.$ At what rate is the area of the square changing when the diagonals are $4\,\text{mm}$ long?"] ["question-08e98843-e2bc-5a10-8ff2-9ed917780859" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each diagonal of the square is increasing at a rate of $1.5\,\text{mm/min},$ so we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=1.5.
$$

Also, when the diagonals are $4\,\text{mm},$ we have $h=4.$ Substituting this information into the above expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=1.5\cdot 4=6{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square increases at $6\,{\text{mm}}^{2}/\text{min}.$"] ["question-08e98843-e2bc-5a10-8ff2-9ed917780859" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] a natural number is the product of the number and all of the natural numbers below it. The factorial of a number is denoted by placing an exclamation point after the number.

For example, the factorial of $4$ is written as $4!$ (with an exclamation point after the $4$), and is computed as

$$
4! = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 24.
$$

So, we say that "four factorial is twenty-four".

The factorials of the natural numbers $1$ through $5$ are as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		1! &= 1 \[5pt]
		2! &= 2 \cdot 1 = 2 \[5pt]	
		3! &= 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 6 \[5pt]	
		4! &= 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 24 \[5pt]	
		5! &= 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 120	
	}
$$

Note that the factorial of $0$ is defined to be equal to $1\mathbin{:}$

$$
0! = 1
$$"] [17592186084445 :tutorial/content "One way to simplify a rational expression containing factorials is to calculate the numerator and denominator separately, and then divide the results. 

For example, computing $\dfrac{10!}{8!}$ using this method, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac {10!}{8!} &= \dfrac {10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} {8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = \dfrac {3\,628\,800} {40\,320} = 90.
	}
$$

However, the method above involves lots of computations. Thankfully, there's an easier way! 

Before we multiply, we can cancel out any numbers that appear in both the numerator and denominator, thereby reducing the amount of computation that's needed. Using this method, we get the same result with far fewer computations:

$$
\require{cancel}

$A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, find the pseudoinverse $A^{+}$."] [17592186159278 :answer-field/choices 17592186159280] [17592186159278 :answer-field/choices 17592186159281] [17592186159278 :answer-field/choices 17592186159282] [17592186159278 :answer-field/choices 17592186159283] [17592186159278 :answer-field/choices 17592186159279] [17592186163306 :tutorial/content "The invertible matrix theorem tells us that if $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix with full rank (i.e., $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$), then there exists a unique inverse matrix $A^{-1}$ such that 

$$
AA^{-1}=A^{-1}\!A=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ denotes the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

There are two questions that we can ask:

- Can we extend the notion of an inverse matrix to one that works for $n\times n$ matrices $A$ where $\mathrm{rank}(A) < n?$

- Is it possible to generalize the concept of an inverse to non-square matrices?

The answer to both questions is yes! This generalization of the inverse of $A$ is called the **pseudoinverse** of $A,$ and is denoted $A^+.$ The dimensions of $A^+$ are the same as $A^T.$

As an example, let's consider the ${\color{red}{3}}\times {\color{blue}{2}}$ matrix $A$ and its corresponding pseudoinverse, given below:

![](images/87/87581a69d3d76dbf3b0ebca8941c9a82b5b9443b00e86f32e4e9e4a42ef5e18b.svg)

- Computing $A^{+}\!A,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+}\,A & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

which is the identity matrix $I_{\color{blue}{2}}.$

- Computing $A\!A^{+},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{+} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which is *almost* the identity matrix $I_{\color{red}{3}}.$

We can explain this result using the following properties of the pseudoinverse:

- *If the columns of an $m\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $A^+A = I_{\color{blue}{n}}.$*

- *If the rows of an ${\color{red}{m}}\times n$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $AA^+ = I_{\color{red}{m}}.$*

In the example above, the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, but the rows are not.

Moreover, the notion of a pseudoinverse is consistent with inverse matrices. In particular,

*If $A$ is an invertible square matrix, then $A^{+} = A^{-1}.$*

$$"] [17592186083926 :question/problem "What is $2!3!$?"] [17592186084444 :tutorial/content "The **factorial** of a natural number is the product of the number and all of the natural numbers below it. The factorial of a number is denoted by placing an exclamation point after the number.

For example, the factorial of $4$ is written as $4$! (with an exclamation point after the $4$), and is computed as

$$
4! = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 24
$$

So, we say that "four factorial is twenty-four".

The factorials of the natural numbers $1$ through $5$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} 1! &= 1 \\[5pt] 2! &= 2 \cdot 1 = 2 \\[5pt] 3! &= 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 6 \\[5pt] 4! &= 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 24 \\[5pt] 5! &= 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 120 \end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned} \dfrac {10!}{8!} &= \dfrac {10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} {8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = \dfrac {3\,628\,800} {40\,320} = 90. \end{aligned}
$$

However, the method above involves lots of computations. Thankfully, there's an easier way!

$$

$$

$$

$$
\require{cancel} \dfrac {10!}{8!} = \dfrac {10 \cdot 9 \cdot \cancel{8!}} {\cancel{8!}} = \dfrac {10 \cdot 9} {1} = 90

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
m∠B &= 2m∠A \\
&= 2(30^{∘}) \\
&= 60^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048826} {:db/id 17592186115627 :question/id #uuid "7ee5fe67-1b69-5908-8440-10420301c716" :question/math-academy-id "q-26920"} {:db/id 17592186115635 :question/id #uuid "4561434b-8603-5c67-b4ad-35c4702a2efd" :question/math-academy-id "q-27351"} {:db/id 17592186115405 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186114981 :question/id #uuid "0c3ef1dc-0262-5bed-9980-1672ca0e6f62" :question/math-academy-id "e-2629"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "13c03056-9692-573f-bf7e-b938ec3a6529" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115637 :question/id #uuid "75b0fb79-6b94-51eb-aaa7-1409425375e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-27363"} {:db/id 17592186115638 :question/id #uuid "6862f91d-e76b-5aae-a439-7d9c5b335b50" :question/math-academy-id "q-27364"}] :knowledge-point/title "Using a Diagram and Properties of Complementary Angles to Find an Unknown Angle"} {:db/id 17592186114981 :question/id #uuid "0c3ef1dc-0262-5bed-9980-1672ca0e6f62" :question/math-academy-id "e-2629" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186115405 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "13c03056-9692-573f-bf7e-b938ec3a6529" :knowledge-point/title "Using a Diagram and Properties of Complementary Angles to Find an Unknown Angle"}] :question/problem "In the figure below, $\angle AOC$ and $\angle COB$ are complementary angles. :step/content {:db/id 17592186079668 :tutorial/content "We've learned two methods for approximating the value of the derivative at a point by computing the rate of change between two points a distance of $h$ apart, where $h$ is small.

- The forward difference approximation computes the rate of change between the point $x$ and the point $x+h,$ which is a step of $h$ units forward.

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)- f(x)}{h}
$$

- The backward difference approximation computes the rate of change between the point $x$ and the point $x-h,$ which is a step of $h$ units backward.

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x)- f(x-h)}{h}
$$

Now, we will introduce the **central difference approximation**, also known as the **symmetric difference approximation**. In this approximation, we compute the rate of change between the points $x-h$ and $x+h,$ a distance of $2h$ apart.

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)- f(x-h)}{2h}
$$

![](images/48/48414a74d6f06fdec0f9b07c2a14f42c3a528b578b3a5f7a61cb4eff93016ac2.png)

Usually, the central difference approximation is a better approximation for $f '(x)$ than the forward difference approximation and the backward difference approximation. This is because for the central difference approximation, $x$ is the midpoint between the two points $x-h$ and $x+h$ that are used in the approximation." :tutorial/id #uuid "Finding Confidence Intervals From Normal Populations"} :step/id #uuid "83fbb490-e605-5aaf-8930-059c037e6897" :step/math-academy-id 37866 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189157}} {:db/id 17592186189092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189369 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a normal population with unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2.$ Recall that a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where $\overline{x}$ is the sample mean, $P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ and $Z \sim N(0,1).$

One thing to realize is that this situation is unrealistic: it's doubtful that we'll not know the population mean yet know the population variance.

A more realistic situation is that $\sigma^2$ is *unknown*, and we must estimate it using the sample data. To estimate the population variance $\sigma^2,$ we use the sample variance $S^2,$ given by

$$
S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2.
$$

It can be shown that 

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n} \sim T_{n-1}
$$

where $T_{n-1}$ is a student's $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

Let's take a look at a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "98d4374a-d448-5d6a-852b-d1d260b9c6bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6241 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "68294170-b618-5346-a481-90c4873ac94a" :step/math-academy-id 37870 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189158}} {:db/id 17592186189093 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189370 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and sample variance $s^2.$ Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} +t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where $P(T > t_{n-1, \alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ and $T \sim T_{n-1}.$ 

The endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\overline{x} \pm t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

- $\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean

- $t_{n-1,\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $t$-score

- $E = t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the margin of error

![](images/10/10cd4a425a9668611335a7e80561944d147faaa9152f91fb9ed87378e8c092eb.svg)

So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{―}{x}-[\text{margin of error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{margin of error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-[\text{[math]t[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{[math]t[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-{t}_{n-1,\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, & \,\overset{―}{x}+{t}_{n-1,\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}})\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the expression for the confidence interval is very similar to when the population variance was known. The only difference is that we now use the $t$-scores instead of $z$-scores and the sample standard deviation $s$ instead of the population standard deviation $\sigma.$

Finally, since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "b3eaa60c-8a64-508a-a094-245270047e8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6242 :tutorial/title "Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Unknown Population Variance"} :step/id #uuid "991795bc-9250-5f2f-96cb-2fb57f170b38" :step/math-academy-id 37871 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189091}} {:db/id 17592186189094 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188284 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186187988 :question/id #uuid "c2e2bcbc-ab4b-5a0a-a803-cb98326017ec" :question/math-academy-id "e-10040"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "778f1426-e8a0-597f-84f6-337359a553c8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188554} {:db/id 17592186188557} {:db/id 17592186502095} {:db/id 17592186502118} {:db/id 17592186502139} {:db/id 17592186502149}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals: Applications"} :step/id #uuid "f1d32a2f-ba24-5d90-9872-8adddcce8f50" :step/math-academy-id 37893} {:db/id 17592186189096 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188285 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186187989 :question/id #uuid "7446f45b-6d41-5a11-8006-853b38fa5142" :question/math-academy-id "e-10047"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "81c8b2bc-d215-5bae-b81f-05870dd39163" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049014}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188553} {:db/id 17592186188558} {:db/id 17592186502087} {:db/id 17592186502102} {:db/id 17592186502111} {:db/id 17592186502116} {:db/id 17592186502135}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals From Large Samples"} :step/id #uuid "c148a2a5-30ac-549d-a5fc-b8016b9a5d06" :step/math-academy-id 37914 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189094}} {:db/id 17592186189157 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189394 :tutorial/content "Up to now, we've assumed that the underlying population is normally distributed. However, if we have a *sufficiently large* sample, then according to the central limit theorem, we have the approximation

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \approx N(0,1).
$$

Moreover, since $n$ is sufficiently large, $\sigma^2$ can be approximated as $S^2.$ Therefore, we have that

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n} \approx T_{n-1}.
$$

**Watch out!** If the population is *not* normally distributed, then the sample size $n$ must be sufficiently large for this approximation to apply. Typically, $n\geq 30$ is sufficient.

In such situations, we can use our formula for the confidence limits of the population mean $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\overline{x} \pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cad33eaf-4573-5886-837e-5a914b347274" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6409 :tutorial/title "Large Samples"} :step/id #uuid "1c95af0f-9fb6-5e0c-89fc-852ce2b16b56" :step/math-academy-id 38729 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189096}} {:db/id 17592186189158 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189395 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=9$ drawn from a normal population. The sample mean is $\overline{x}=30,$ and the sample standard deviation is $s=3.3.$ 
We wish to compute a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu.$

Recall that a confidence interval is an interval of the form 

$$
(\overline{x}-E, \: \overline{x}+E),
$$

 

where 

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean, and

- $E$ is the margin of error.

In our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is also normally distributed, where

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

By transforming $\overline{X}$ in the manner described earlier, we have that the random variable $T,$ defined as

$$
T = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n},
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution $T_{n-1}$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

We wish to find a $t$-interval that we're $95\%$ confident that the random variable $T$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

![](images/63/63973d7f59a993d42b7b8145f3354e9e7d7dba3c0393c756b6a95754eb4ead2e.png)

  

Since we wish to find a $95\%$ confidence interval, we define our parameter $\alpha$ as 

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.
$$

Notice that $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\pm t_{n-1, \alpha/2}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/b5/b557afdbd649aa159addd9fe01021a7c3561f94b0168fd874876980d8bb7c3f4.png)

  

According to our diagram,

$$
P(T > t_{8,0.025}) = P(T < -t_{8,0.025}) = 0.025.
$$

  

Using a table of values for the $t$-distribution, we find that $t_{8,0.025} \approx 2.306.$ Therefore,

$$
P(T > 2.306) = P(T < -2.306) = 0.025.
$$

In other words,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-2.306<T<2.306)=0.95\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, there is a $95\%$ probability that our random variable $T$ will lie in the interval $(-2.306, 2.306).$

Similar to the case where $\sigma^2$ was known, we find the appropriate confidence interval by solving the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2.306 & <T<2.306 \\ -2.306 & <\frac{\overset{―}{x}-\mu }{s/\sqrt{n}}<2.306 \\ -2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} & <\overset{―}{x}-\mu <2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \\ -\overset{―}{x}-2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} & <-\mu <-\overset{―}{x}+2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}+2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} & >\mu >\overset{―}{x}-2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}-2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} & <\mu <\overset{―}{x}+2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

   

Therefore, a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x}-2.306 \cdot\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x}+2.306 \cdot\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}  \right).
$$

Finally, substituting our values

$$
n=9, \qquad
\overline{x}=30, \qquad
s=3.3,
$$

we obtain that our $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is 

$$
\big( 30- 2.537, \: 30 + 2.537 \big).
$$

 

Describing this confidence interval using confidence limits, we have

$$
30 \pm 2.537.
$$

Let's now describe the general procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "3941a0da-320f-5a13-b99f-f3556ba560ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6410 :tutorial/title "Constructing Confidence Intervals"} :step/id #uuid "a7e1e894-dda6-51e5-9fc8-542ca1fec109" :step/math-academy-id 38730 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189093}}] :activity/title "Confidence Intervals for One Mean: Unknown Population Variance" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186188450} {:db/id 17592186189092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189369 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a normal population with unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2.$ Recall that a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

Finally, since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "b3eaa60c-8a64-508a-a094-245270047e8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6242 :tutorial/title "Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Unknown Population Variance"} :step/id #uuid "991795bc-9250-5f2f-96cb-2fb57f170b38" :step/math-academy-id 37871 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189091}} {:db/id 17592186189370 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and sample variance $s^2.$ Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} +t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where $P(T > t_{n-1, \alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ and $T \sim T_{n-1}.$ 

The endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\overline{x} \pm t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

- $\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean

- $t_{n-1,\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $t$-score

- $E = t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the margin of error

![](images/10/10cd4a425a9668611335a7e80561944d147faaa9152f91fb9ed87378e8c092eb.svg)

So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{―}{x}-[\text{margin of error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{margin of error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-[\text{[math]t[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{[math]t[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-{t}_{n-1,\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, & \,\overset{―}{x}+{t}_{n-1,\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}})\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the expression for the confidence interval is very similar to when the population variance was known. The only difference is that we now use the $t$-scores instead of $z$-scores and the sample standard deviation $s$ instead of the population standard deviation $\sigma.$

Finally, since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "b3eaa60c-8a64-508a-a094-245270047e8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6242 :tutorial/title "Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Unknown Population Variance"} {:db/id 17592186189094 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188284 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186187988 :question/id #uuid "c2e2bcbc-ab4b-5a0a-a803-cb98326017ec" :question/math-academy-id "e-10040"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "778f1426-e8a0-597f-84f6-337359a553c8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188554} {:db/id 17592186188557} {:db/id 17592186502095} {:db/id 17592186502118} {:db/id 17592186502139} {:db/id 17592186502149}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals: Applications"} :step/id #uuid "f1d32a2f-ba24-5d90-9872-8adddcce8f50" :step/math-academy-id 37893} {:db/id 17592186189096 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188285 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186187989 :question/id #uuid "7446f45b-6d41-5a11-8006-853b38fa5142" :question/math-academy-id "e-10047"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "81c8b2bc-d215-5bae-b81f-05870dd39163" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049014}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188553} {:db/id 17592186188558} {:db/id 17592186502087} {:db/id 17592186502102} {:db/id 17592186502111} {:db/id 17592186502116} {:db/id 17592186502135}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals From Large Samples"} :step/id #uuid "c148a2a5-30ac-549d-a5fc-b8016b9a5d06" :step/math-academy-id 37914 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189094}} {:db/id 17592186189394 :tutorial/content "Up to now, we've assumed that the underlying population is normally distributed. However, if we have a *sufficiently large* sample, then according to the central limit theorem, we have the approximation

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \approx N(0,1).
$$

Moreover, since $n$ is sufficiently large, $\sigma^2$ can be approximated as $S^2.$ Therefore, we have that

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n} \approx T_{n-1}.
$$

**Watch out!** If the population is *not* normally distributed, then the sample size $n$ must be sufficiently large for this approximation to apply. Typically, $n\geq 30$ is sufficient.

In such situations, we can use our formula for the confidence limits of the population mean $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\overline{x} \pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cad33eaf-4573-5886-837e-5a914b347274" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6409 :tutorial/title "Large Samples"} {:db/id 17592186189395 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=9$ drawn from a normal population. The sample mean is $\overline{x}=30,$ and the sample standard deviation is $s=3.3.$ 
We wish to compute a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu.$

Recall that a confidence interval is an interval of the form 

$$
(\overline{x}-E, \: \overline{x}+E),
$$

 

where 

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean, and

- $E$ is the margin of error.

In our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is also normally distributed, where

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

By transforming $\overline{X}$ in the manner described earlier, we have that the random variable $T,$ defined as

$$
T = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n},
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution $T_{n-1}$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

We wish to find a $t$-interval that we're $95\%$ confident that the random variable $T$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

![](images/63/63973d7f59a993d42b7b8145f3354e9e7d7dba3c0393c756b6a95754eb4ead2e.png)

  

Since we wish to find a $95\%$ confidence interval, we define our parameter $\alpha$ as 

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.
$$

Notice that $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\pm t_{n-1, \alpha/2}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/b5/b557afdbd649aa159addd9fe01021a7c3561f94b0168fd874876980d8bb7c3f4.png)

  

According to our diagram,

$$
P(T > t_{8,0.025}) = P(T < -t_{8,0.025}) = 0.025.
$$

  

Using a table of values for the $t$-distribution, we find that $t_{8,0.025} \approx 2.306.$ Therefore,

$$
P(T > 2.306) = P(T < -2.306) = 0.025.
$$

In other words,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-2.306<T<2.306)=0.95\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, there is a $95\%$ probability that our random variable $T$ will lie in the interval $(-2.306, 2.306).$

Similar to the case where $\sigma^2$ was known, we find the appropriate confidence interval by solving the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2.306 & <T<2.306 \\ -2.306 & <\frac{\overset{―}{x}-\mu }{s/\sqrt{n}}<2.306 \\ -2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} & <\overset{―}{x}-\mu <2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \\ -\overset{―}{x}-2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} & <-\mu <-\overset{―}{x}+2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}+2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} & >\mu >\overset{―}{x}-2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}-2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} & <\mu <\overset{―}{x}+2.306\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

   

Therefore, a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x}-2.306 \cdot\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x}+2.306 \cdot\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}  \right).
$$

Finally, substituting our values

$$
n=9, \qquad
\overline{x}=30, \qquad
s=3.3,
$$

we obtain that our $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is 

$$
\big( 30- 2.537, \: 30 + 2.537 \big).
$$

 

Describing this confidence interval using confidence limits, we have

$$
30 \pm 2.537.
$$

Let's now describe the general procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "3941a0da-320f-5a13-b99f-f3556ba560ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6410 :tutorial/title "Constructing Confidence Intervals"} {:course/id We count the number of pentagons. We see that there are $4$ pentagons.

So the ratio of triangles to pentagons is $2:4.$

We can simplify this ratio by dividing both numbers in a ratio by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,4 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,\,2 &  &  &  & \,\,\,↓÷\,\,2 &  \\ \,\,1 &  & : &  & \,\,\,2 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ratio of triangles to pentagons is $1:2.$"} {:db/id 17592186515552 :question/id #uuid "65505664-38a4-5c26-b1d6-fe28649569b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-59891"} {:db/id 17592186073740 $$

$$

Now, let's consider each of the given digits we can substitute into the blank.

$$
2:6
$$

If we multiply *both* numbers by $5,$ for example, we get the ratio $10:30.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,6 &  \\ \,\,↓\times \,5 &  &  &  & \,\,↓\times \,5 &  \\ \,10 &  & : &  & \,30 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ratios $2:6$ and $10:30$ are equivalent. 

Similarly, if we take the ratio $2:6$ and divide *both* numbers by $2,$ we get $1:3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,6 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,2 &  &  &  & \,\,↓÷\,2 &  \\ \,\,1 &  & : &  & \,\,3 & \end{aligned}
$$

"cbbdf6cb-f6ca-5deb-b060-a316432db0ee" :topic/math-academy-id 327} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065131 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065412 :tutorial/content "When we subtract a positive number from another positive number, we move towards the left on the number line. 

For example, let's consider the following subtraction problem:

$$
3 - 5
$$

To subtract $5$ from $3,$ we start at $3$ on the number line and move $5$ places to the left.

![](images/57/57ac1fe7a28ae5fefadf900d2276d499cdccf01df48b819b0aafa5347a2ec506.png)

When we do this, we land at $-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
3-5 = -2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8af27dde-6aa4-5067-84f8-9538f1acaa18" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8029 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e99d8d22-f103-5560-a608-35f0957133f4" :step/math-academy-id 188374 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065132}} {:db/id 17592186065132 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064255 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063935 :question/id #uuid "34280e7c-023c-5c7f-b22b-3f322ff97dad" :question/math-academy-id "e-12813"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6a3c970b-4086-52ef-ac0f-2b8c3d72fd51" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049429}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064527} {:db/id 17592186064570} {:db/id 17592186064629} {:db/id 17592186433314} {:db/id 17592186433317} {:db/id 17592186433318} {:db/id 17592186433319} {:db/id 17592186433320} {:db/id 17592186515582}] :knowledge-point/title "Subtracting a Positive Number From a Non-Negative Number"} :step/id #uuid "a7e8a41f-1f30-5c54-b22b-c51e7a5efd82" :step/math-academy-id 188375 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065133}} {:db/id 17592186065133 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065413 :tutorial/content "It is impractical to use number lines to subtract large numbers. 

However, a neat trick makes subtracting a positive number from a smaller positive number very easy!

As an example, let's consider the following subtraction problem:

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}}
$$

Since $68$ is larger than $37,$ the answer *must be negative*.

We start by solving an easier problem: subtracting the numbers *in the reverse order*. In our case, the reverse problem is

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}}.
$$

Next, we carry out the subtraction:

![](images/db/db192e5c1f089e3d4cc2a7b1238392e44a7ba36bff99345a997042c16ebc304f.svg)

So, we have

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}} = 31.
$$

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above. 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}} = -31.
$$

However, a neat trick makes subtracting a positive number from a smaller positive number very easy!

As an example, let's consider the following subtraction problem:

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}}
$$

Since $68$ is larger than $37,$ the answer *must be negative*.

We start by solving an easier problem: subtracting the numbers *in the reverse order*. In our case, the reverse problem is

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}}.
$$

Next, we carry out the subtraction:

![](images/db/db192e5c1f089e3d4cc2a7b1238392e44a7ba36bff99345a997042c16ebc304f.svg)

So, we have

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}} = 31.
$$

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above. 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}} = -31.
$$

And that's it! 

Let's use the same idea to subtract two three-digit numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "d7dbb60e-47d5-56db-981a-145c532f7ace" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8030 :tutorial/title "Subtraction With Larger Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "12b96179-bf32-5136-bbf1-e7631a656dfb" :step/math-academy-id 188379 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065134}} {:db/id 17592186065413 :tutorial/content "It is impractical to use number lines to subtract large numbers.

The first rule says that when we multiply a negative number by a positive number, the result (**product**) is a negative number. We can picture this multiplication rule as

$$
(-)\cdot(+) = (-)or(+)\cdot(-) = (-)
$$

For instance, let's find out the value of $(-3) \cdot 10$.
Here, we have a product of a negative number $\color{red}(-3)$ and a positive one ${\color{blue}(10)}$. So the product will be negative:
$30$
Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we multiply $3$ by $10$ without any signs:

$$
3 \cdot 10 = 30
$$

So, we get

$$
{\color{red}(-3)} \cdot {\color{blue}10} = {\color{red} -30}
$$

Note that multiplication is **commutative**, meaning it doesn't matter in what order we multiply two numbers. Commutativity means that we're allowed to swap the numbers, which gives

$$
{\color{red}(-3)} \cdot {\color{blue}10} = {\color{blue}10}\cdot {\color{red}(-3)} = {\color{red} -30}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1eb02261-90e4-51bc-a24e-dabdedaafa63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8105 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "480bb98f-29a4-57e1-9342-972680f415f8" :step/math-academy-id 82238 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065294}} {:db/id 17592186065294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064363 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063939 :question/id #uuid "9e3473f6-80c1-5559-b29f-ac0bcb2f3a13" :question/math-academy-id "e-12967"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "75901336-1d0e-51f1-acde-d6eb784d9f82" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049429}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064550} {:db/id 17592186064576} {:db/id 17592186432267} {:db/id 17592186432268} {:db/id 17592186518121}] :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying a Positive Number by a Negative Number"} :step/id #uuid "cb9bb839-e0dc-5aca-9cc9-ae22d07a3486" :step/math-academy-id 82239 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065295}} {:db/id 17592186065295 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064364 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063940 :question/id #uuid "e4e645fe-d1cd-584c-b6a3-4e75e1170a34" :question/math-academy-id "e-12969"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9cb97145-a93a-5df3-8dbe-6777d21601c8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186051030}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064767} {:db/id 17592186064940} {:db/id 17592186064974} {:db/id 17592186424824} {:db/id 17592186432266} {:db/id 17592186515611}] :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying a Positive Number by a Negative Number With Decimals"} :step/id #uuid "b387ed41-0522-5959-a882-fcd13a445bf5" :step/math-academy-id 82242}] :activity/title "Multiplying Positive Numbers With Negative Numbers" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064401} {:db/id 17592186065293 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065415 :tutorial/content "Multiplying with negative numbers can be summed up by two simple rules.
