17592186167884}} {:db/id 17592186167879 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168016 :tutorial/content "Recall that the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

Notice that the second component of the third equilibrium point is positive only when 

$$
h < \dfrac{d}{c},
$$

which guarantees that the third fixed point will lie in the first quadrant. For now, let's consider only this case.

We now evaluate the Jacobian matrix
![](images/89/89ca57d2d308201a46a31695c27ad866604ef4f230609ad3047e186824e5dc28.svg)
at the nonzero equilibrium ![](images/f2/f2965d33d48e48fa977e876803aa3da55c1c47c3569a24cb8341b97ba43420c2.svg) to get

![](images/b2/b239f1170a7bf5a5f6ad6043492aa0772adcc2a53e7f3ebdad15ad195b1520d9.svg)

Because we are considering the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ we have that

$$
\dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = -a < 0$ and $\lambda_2 = \dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Analyzing the type of the third equilibrium in full generality becomes considerably more cumbersome. Therefore, we'll examine a concrete example later in the lesson. For now, we simply note that the third equilibrium is an *asymptotically stable (spiral) sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c82332ed5277586a2b97e900383619a5d61cdb73ff4b60a92de3d5460165165.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](images/a7/a7673170825344e1831f2ba01ce4c20f10091380ff4e116f3b6bd9e7666e51aa.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "4ce000cd-7913-5e8e-90d2-3a5a820db4f4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14543 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Nonzero Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b61ca7e0-a217-5555-8d14-3f0d56453cb5" :step/math-academy-id 590167 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167885}} {:db/id 17592186167880 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166928 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166559 :question/id #uuid "3e280ec5-c95a-5ca6-ba2e-edc4cf653ea3" :question/math-academy-id "e-21736"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4936474f-5e5f-5da2-8242-1b48336a836c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048881}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167252} {:db/id 17592186167261} {:db/id 17592186370423} {:db/id 17592186370540} {:db/id 17592186480691} {:db/id 17592186497388}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case"} :step/id #uuid "33bb23bb-bd23-5d38-9487-0ff5ffdddc57" :step/math-academy-id 590168 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167881}} {:db/id 17592186167881 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168017 :tutorial/content "Again, recall that the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

We have already considered the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ which guarantees that the third equilibrium will lie in the first quadrant. Let's now consider the remaining cases.

- When $h = \dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium coincides with the second one. So, we have only two equilibria:

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right) = \left(\dfrac{c}{d}, 0\right)
$$

- When $h > \dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium is in the fourth quadrant (its $y$-coordinate is negative). So, we have only two equilibria that make sense in the context of the model:

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

Hence, we get only two equilibria. 

The trajectories near the origin remain similar. However, the equilibrium at

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

will be an *asymptotically stable sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h \geq \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](images/b9/b94beebb63bc1312d56f655e48b3bc7cdb1b9badc5cdacd6b88b073c5055adc9.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](images/cd/cd60f32a5daff3c805b097d121814d19e04781ed1bcfead989cde82db674e5d9.png)

Eventually, the *predators go extinct* while the prey approaches the carrying capacity of the system.

Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "92ed0e52-b2f2-5d81-99c3-60526aa8f13a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14547 :tutorial/title "Predator Extinction Case"} :step/id #uuid "0b301d8f-79ee-5a20-babe-fd63b54fd69b" :step/math-academy-id 590172 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167882}} {:db/id 17592186167882 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166929 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166560 :question/id #uuid "3076e962-385d-5c19-8179-7c1a91aa6e55" :question/math-academy-id "e-21738"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b87aeba5-eb67-5dc0-9c25-d9c1cefdb6e2" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167253} {:db/id 17592186167254} {:db/id 17592186370462} {:db/id 17592186370501} {:db/id 17592186402168} {:db/id 17592186480649} {:db/id 17592186480690} {:db/id 17592186497413}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Predator Extinction Case"} :step/id #uuid "51d64692-6d2f-5189-bd9c-6590b8925293" :step/math-academy-id 590173} {:db/id 17592186167883 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168028 :tutorial/content "Recall that the equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, for the Lotka–Volterra model 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bxy=0 \\ -cy+dxy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=\dfrac{c}{d}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bx(0) & =0 \\ ax(1-hx) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$

- If $x=\dfrac{c}{d},$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{c}{d})(1-h(\frac{c}{d}))-b(\frac{c}{d})y & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h)-by & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h) & =by \\ y & =\frac{a}{b}(1-\frac{c}{d}h).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "79e78f76-a29e-544f-a86b-9f714e69cf63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14597 :tutorial/title "Equilibrium Points"} :step/id #uuid "f7c2a3b7-bd87-5cba-ba5e-ea5beeed7071" :step/math-academy-id 590177 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167878}} {:db/id 17592186167884 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168029 :tutorial/content "Consider the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\,-\,2hx)-by, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/1d/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/03/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get

![](images/cf/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Thus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model." :tutorial/id #uuid "feef6e7a-79a2-5b71-8cec-dc45e305ec52" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14598 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Origin"} :step/id #uuid "8118c930-2041-5a97-bb4f-5812d27ead9b" :step/math-academy-id 590178 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167879}} {:db/id 17592186167885 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168030 :tutorial/content "Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=4x(1-0.25x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-2y+3xy\end{aligned}
$$

We'll evaluate its Jacobian at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[4, \, 0]^T$ that lies on the $x$-axis.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=4x(1-0.25x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-2y+3xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=4-2x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/0b/0bd1edc4527b82bebf84d38f8d4a79b65062d6b38c5fa4c84b7509acaa547f42.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/30/30463f939876ccbee7cf77f8fdc80fb4e8a27fe0ad5af22cd51e1be3433a3af5.svg) to get

![](images/fc/fc40e7e568705e08b70e0dedae710b2e8514837491730ae12a90bed764261f97.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = 10$ and $\lambda_2=-4$. Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, 

- $x=x(t)$ is the *prey population*, and

- $y=y(t)$ is the *predator population*.

The only difference from the Lotka–Volterra model is the factor $(1-hx)$ in the prey equation. Notice that if $h=0,$ we get the standard model:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

In our modified version of the model, the *intrinsic growth* of prey is given by the $ax(1-hx)$ term. Now, if there are no predators ($y=0$), then 

$$
x' = ax(1-hx).
$$

Recall that general solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,\frac{1}{h}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{h}.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the *carrying capacity* (the limit the number of prey is approaching as $t$ goes to infinity).

![](images/8b/8b7a6d12af77f6c2d2e6d3596e71a51a3d697a5c28e9f9c64c5675a01df812d5.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "d7c622bc-33ae-5782-8c5f-cb14af0d21e2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14542 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0fbe051e-af21-5ed1-a3d3-ed273a110dd2" :step/math-academy-id 590160 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167877}} {:db/id 17592186168015 :tutorial/content "The Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with **carrying capacity** is given by

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bxy=0 \\ -cy+dxy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=\dfrac{c}{d}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bx(0) & =0 \\ ax(1-hx) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$

- If $x=\dfrac{c}{d},$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{c}{d})(1-h(\frac{c}{d}))-b(\frac{c}{d})y & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h)-by & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h) & =by \\ y & =\frac{a}{b}(1-\frac{c}{d}h).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "79e78f76-a29e-544f-a86b-9f714e69cf63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14597 :tutorial/title "Equilibrium Points"} :step/id #uuid "f7c2a3b7-bd87-5cba-ba5e-ea5beeed7071" :step/math-academy-id 590177 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167878}} {:db/id 17592186167878 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166927 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166558 :question/id #uuid "b7cba6bc-39b5-5e03-ba33-c1fc2a1b4ae8" :question/math-academy-id "e-21735"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c444e892-e49f-5ea7-9ac9-c51078566c40" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048990}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167251} {:db/id 17592186167260} {:db/id 17592186370395} {:db/id 17592186370402} {:db/id 17592186370409} {:db/id 17592186370416} {:db/id 17592186480667} {:db/id 17592186480707} {:db/id 17592186497359}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Equilibrium Points of the Modified Lotka-Volterra System"} :step/id #uuid "4ee40fef-c655-575b-86ae-0bef94e43fec" :step/math-academy-id 590164 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167884}} {:db/id 17592186167884 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168029 :tutorial/content "Consider the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\,-\,2hx)-by, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/1d/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/03/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get

![](images/cf/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Thus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model." :tutorial/id #uuid "feef6e7a-79a2-5b71-8cec-dc45e305ec52" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14598 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Origin"} :step/id #uuid "8118c930-2041-5a97-bb4f-5812d27ead9b" :step/math-academy-id 590178 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167879}} {:db/id 17592186167879 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168016 :tutorial/content "Recall that the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

Notice that the second component of the third equilibrium point is positive only when 

$$
h < \dfrac{d}{c},
$$

which guarantees that the third fixed point will lie in the first quadrant. For now, let's consider only this case.

We now evaluate the Jacobian matrix
![](images/89/89ca57d2d308201a46a31695c27ad866604ef4f230609ad3047e186824e5dc28.svg)
at the nonzero equilibrium ![](images/f2/f2965d33d48e48fa977e876803aa3da55c1c47c3569a24cb8341b97ba43420c2.svg) to get

![](images/b2/b239f1170a7bf5a5f6ad6043492aa0772adcc2a53e7f3ebdad15ad195b1520d9.svg)

Because we are considering the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ we have that

$$
\dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = -a < 0$ and $\lambda_2 = \dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Analyzing the type of the third equilibrium in full generality becomes considerably more cumbersome. Therefore, we'll examine a concrete example later in the lesson. For now, we simply note that the third equilibrium is an *asymptotically stable (spiral) sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c82332ed5277586a2b97e900383619a5d61cdb73ff4b60a92de3d5460165165.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bxy=0 \\ -cy+dxy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=\dfrac{c}{d}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bx(0) & =0 \\ ax(1-hx) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$

- If $x=\dfrac{c}{d},$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{c}{d})(1-h(\frac{c}{d}))-b(\frac{c}{d})y & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h)-by & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h) & =by \\ y & =\frac{a}{b}(1-\frac{c}{d}h).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "79e78f76-a29e-544f-a86b-9f714e69cf63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14597 :tutorial/title "Equilibrium Points"} {:db/id 17592186168029 :tutorial/content "Consider the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\,-\,2hx)-by, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/1d/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/03/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get

![](images/cf/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Thus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model." :tutorial/id #uuid "feef6e7a-79a2-5b71-8cec-dc45e305ec52" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14598 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Origin"} {:db/id 17592186168030 :tutorial/content "Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$

We'll evaluate its Jacobian at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[4, \, 0]^T$ that lies on the $x$-axis.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=4x(1-0.25x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-2y+3xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x(1-2x)-xy)=5-20x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}5-20x-y & -x \\ 3y & -2+3x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}5-20(0)-0 & -0 \\ 3(0) & -2+3(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$"} :step/id #uuid "5932a145-7c28-5526-882d-17efb83e0fb8"} {:db/id 17592186497459 :step/content {:db/id 17592186370416 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b0cca672-22d2-56b4-8615-61d6e24b7f94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186370418}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370418} :answer-field/id #uuid "07b070e5-7be6-50e8-a4a0-beb9ca54ef6f" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186370417} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dda70e62-0307-5f61-be89-38a5799d0f0e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186370420}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370420} :answer-field/id #uuid "793a6dcc-2165-52e4-94f6-60749fcac9b0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186370419} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3512a5da-77e9-5ff0-a44a-28af35917f39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186370422}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370422} :answer-field/id #uuid "f1e028e8-2b52-5edb-aa50-089cf299893a" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186370421}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6734dc20-5e4c-5ba3-a922-996f26cded96" :question/math-academy-id "q-335607" :question/problem "$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-2xy=0 \\ -6y+3xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6y+3xy & =0 \\ y(-6+3x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-2x(0) & =0 \\ 4x(0.25x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(4,0).$

- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4(2)(1-0.25(2))-2(2)y & =0 \\ 4-4y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2,1).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0),\,(4,0),\,(2,1).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9c6eefcd-5b2a-58f2-8fa4-3bbf0349123c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497435}} {:db/id 17592186497473 :step/content {:db/id 17592186497359 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ac7f7168-2238-5278-920a-322ccf51d756" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186497010}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186497010} :answer-field/id #uuid "2827ddbf-479b-5003-a2de-01715d6851fe" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186497233} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7038e05b-62e6-5b9d-89f6-5884cc66e3ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186496900}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496900} :answer-field/id #uuid "866fb4cc-629f-52ec-a9a5-882783d95536" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186497280} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "56c313eb-74f2-5951-b106-ca3f0b7a9669" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186496841}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496841} :answer-field/id #uuid "a9119afb-d7f2-5573-9b5d-ea702cbc65cd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186497295}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "54e98471-5688-5240-867b-3e9eae0b3046" :question/math-academy-id "q-335588" :question/problem "$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x(1-x)-2xy)=2-4x-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x(1-x)-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}2-4x-2y & -2x \\ 3y & -2+3x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2-4(0)-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 3(0) & -2+3(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x(1-2x)-xy)=5-20x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}5-20x-y & -x \\ 3y & -2+3x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}5-20(0)-0 & -0 \\ 3(0) & -2+3(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$(0,0),\,(${{field-1}}$,0),\,(${{field-2}}$,${{field-3}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-2xy=0 \\ -6y+3xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6y+3xy & =0 \\ y(-6+3x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3x^{4} + 7x^{3} - 10x + 8}{-3x + 2} &= (3x^{4} + 7x^{3} - 10x + 8)/(-3(x - \frac{2}{3})) \\
&=-\frac{1}{3}((3x^{4} + 7x^{3} - 10x + 8)/((x - \frac{2}{3})))
\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on

$$
\dfrac{3x^4+7x^3-10x+8}{\left(x-\frac23\right)}
$$

remembering to include a coefficient of zero for the $x^2$ term, we arrive at the following:

$$
\frac{2}{3}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 7 & 0 & -10\end{vmatrix}8; 2\begin{vmatrix}6 & 4 & -4 \\ 3 & 9 & 6\end{vmatrix}- 6 \mid 4
$$

Reading off the bottom row, we get

$$
\frac{3x^4+7x^3-10x+8}{\left(x-\frac23\right)} = 3x^3+9x^2+6x-6+\frac{4}{\left(x-\frac23\right)}
$$

Finally, we multiply by the original

$$
-\dfrac 1 3
$$

factor to get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3x^{4} + 7x^{3} - 10x + 8}{2 - 3x} &= -\frac{1}{3}(3x^{3} + 9x^{2} + 6x - 6 + (4)/((x - \frac{2}{3}))) \\
&=-x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 2x + 2 + \frac{4}{2 - 3x}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186051079} {:db/id 17592186083596 :question/id #uuid "862efaba-0574-5254-813c-1a078cf1c758" :question/math-academy-id "q-19108"} {:db/id 17592186083597 :question/id #uuid "c2b65857-f961-5afd-9ef2-0421d5a69f7a" :question/math-academy-id "q-19186" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186083204 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2b0a87cd-e9b5-5ca1-8132-b62a715264ac" :knowledge-point/title "Dividing a Polynomial by a Linear Binomial With Leading Coefficients"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cf342cce-75a0-51e5-9b74-c5d653177672" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3x - $$
\dfrac{2x^3-5x^2-7x+11}{x-3}
$$

To do this, we can use **synthetic division**. Synthetic division allows us to divide a polynomial by a factor of the form $(x-c)$. Here's how we do it.

| $3\begin{vmatrix}2 & -5 & -7\end{vmatrix}11$ | Start off by writing the term $c$ of the divisor on the left side. Here, $c = {\color{blue}{3}}$. Then, write the coefficients of all terms of the dividend on the right side in descending order of their degree. Remember the sign! Also, if a term is missing, use $0$ as the coefficient. |
| --- | ---: |
| $3\begin{vmatrix}2 & -5 & -7\end{vmatrix}11; ↓; 2$ | Bring down the leading term of the dividend. Here, the leading term is ${\color{red}2}$. |
| $3\begin{vmatrix}2 & -5 & -7\end{vmatrix}11; 6; 2$ | Multiply the leading term $\color{red}2$ by ${\color{blue}3}$. This gives ${{\color{blue}{3}}\cdot \color{red}{2}} = {\color{green}6}$. Place the result below the next term. |
| $3\begin{vmatrix}2 & -5 & -7\end{vmatrix}11; 6; 2 \mid 1$ | Add the last result ($\color{green}{6}$) to the term located above ($\color{magenta}{-5}$) and write their sum below the line. This gives ${\color{magenta}{-5}} + {\color{green}{6}}={\color{red}{1}}$. |
| $3\begin{vmatrix}2 & -5 & -7\end{vmatrix}11; 6\begin{vmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{vmatrix}1$ | We now repeat the process. Multiply the last result ($\color{red}1$ here) by $\color{blue} 3$ and place the result below the next term. This gives ${\color{blue}{3}}\cdot {\color{red}{1}}= {\color{green}{3}}$. |
| $3\begin{vmatrix}2 & -5 & -7\end{vmatrix}11; 6\begin{vmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{vmatrix}1 \mid - 4$ | Now add the last result ($\color{green}{3}$) to the term located above ($\color{magenta}{-7}$) and write their sum below the line. This gives ${\color{magenta}{-7}} + {\color{green}{3}}={\color{red}{-4}}$. |
| $3\begin{vmatrix}2 & -5 & -7\end{vmatrix}11; 6\begin{vmatrix}3 & -12 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}- 4 \mid - 1$ | There is one last step. Again, multiply $\color{blue} 3$ by the last result $\color{red}-4$ and write it below the constant term. This gives ${\color{blue}{3}}\cdot{\color{red}{(-4)}}={\color{green}-12}$. Finally, add $\color{green}-12$ to $\color{magenta}11$ to get ${\color{blue}{-1}}$, which is the remainder. The remainder $\color{blue}-1$ is important, so we put a box around it. |

The numbers $2$, $1$ and $-4$ in the bottom row are the coefficients of the **quotient**. So from left to right, the quotient is

$$
2x^2+1x-4
$$

The **remainder** is the value in the box, so ${\color{blue}-1}$ in this case.

Finally, we can write the full result of the division as

$$
\dfrac{2x^3-5x^2-7x+11}{x-3}=2x^2+x-4+\dfrac{\color{blue}-1}{x-3}
$$

which simplifies to

$$
\dfrac{2x^3-5x^2-7x+11}{x-3}=2x^2+x-4-\dfrac{1}{x-3}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a99cb4a9-8428-584f-bcab-c2806d04719d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3383 :tutorial/title "Dividing a Polynomial Using Synthetic Division"} :step/id #uuid "7e09c9d5-51c1-52a9-a8a2-2acf0b38cd4d" :step/math-academy-id 18899 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084273}} {:db/id 17592186084089 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083203 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186083004 :question/id #uuid "551cceca-a69f-57c1-b4b0-c8f7aedd3cdc" :question/math-academy-id "e-5146"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c47216a0-3e51-50bb-b7eb-f92592db5dbc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049538}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083822} {:db/id 17592186083930}] :knowledge-point/title "Dividing a Polynomial by a Linear Binomial Using Synthetic Division"} :step/id #uuid "7b4de1ae-1152-53f5-a47b-143b708404f8" :step/math-academy-id 18901 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084090}} {:db/id 17592186084090 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084440 :tutorial/content "We have already seen how synthetic division can be used to quickly divide a polynomial by a linear binomial with a leading coefficient of $1$.

In fact, synthetic division can be used when the divisor is *any* linear binomial, like $(ax+b)$. We just factor out the leading coefficient $a$, carry out the division in the standard way, and then include the leading coefficient in the final result.

$$
\dfrac{2x^3-5x^2-7x+11}{x-3}
$$

First, let's get familiar with some terminology:

- The **dividend** is the polynomial that we want to divide, so $2x^3-5x^2-7x+11$ in this case.
- The **divisor** is the polynomial that we want to divide the dividend by, so $x-3$ in this case.
- The result of the division, which will be a polynomial, is called the **quotient**.
- The **remainder** is what is left after the division.

Before we start, we need to check that the polynomials are written in standard form. In our case, the terms in both the numerator and denominator are in descending order of their degree, so we're ready to go!" :tutorial/id #uuid "0402dd10-0c81-5ad3-b813-6af9d4fe5fbc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3928 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c1e715a2-551a-5990-b6c4-823e40d008ec" :step/math-academy-id 23194 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084088}} {:db/id 17592186084273 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084483 :tutorial/content "Dividing $2x^3-5x^2-7x+11$ by $x-3$, we obtained that

$$
\dfrac{2x^3-5x^2-7x+11}{x-3}=2x^2+x-4-\dfrac{1}{x-3}
$$

Now, multiplying both sides by $x-3$, we get

$$
{\color{blue}2x^3-5x^2-7x+11}=(x-3)(2x^2+x-4)-1
$$

Therefore, to check if we have done the division correctly, we can simply multiply the polynomials on the right-hand side and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x - 3)(2x^{2} + x - 4) - 1 &= x(2x^{2} + x - 4) - 3(2x^{2} + x - 4) - 1 \\
&= 2x^{3} + x^{2} - 4x - 6x^{2} - 3x + 12 - 1 \\
&= 2x^{3} - 5x^{2} - 7x + 11✓
\end{aligned}

$$
\dfrac{2x^3-5x^2-7x+11}{x-3}
$$

First, let's get familiar with some terminology:

- The **dividend** is the polynomial that we want to divide, so $2x^3-5x^2-7x+11$ in this case.
- The **divisor** is the polynomial that we want to divide the dividend by, so $x-3$ in this case.
- The result of the division, which will be a polynomial, is called the **quotient**.
- The **remainder** is what is left after the division.

Before we start, we need to check that the polynomials are written in standard form. In our case, the terms in both the numerator and denominator are in descending order of their degree, so we're ready to go!" :tutorial/id #uuid "0402dd10-0c81-5ad3-b813-6af9d4fe5fbc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3928 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186084483 :tutorial/content "Dividing $2x^3-5x^2-7x+11$ by $x-3$, we obtained that

$$
\dfrac{2x^3-5x^2-7x+11}{x-3}=2x^2+x-4-\dfrac{1}{x-3}
$$

Now, multiplying both sides by $x-3$, we get

$$
{\color{blue}2x^3-5x^2-7x+11}=(x-3)(2x^2+x-4)-1
$$

Therefore, to check if we have done the division correctly, we can simply multiply the polynomials on the right-hand side and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x - 3)(2x^{2} + x - 4) - 1 &= x(2x^{2} + x - 4) - 3(2x^{2} + x - 4) - 1 \\
&= 2x^{3} + x^{2} - 4x - 6x^{2} - 3x + 12 - 1 \\
&= 2x^{3} - 5x^{2} - 7x + 11✓
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2e9f9179-dc6d-5214-a258-b8b1d6900457" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4984 :tutorial/title "Checking the Division"} {:db/id 17592186050411 :topic/difficulty 1.4422504997939773 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428792 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. A graphic designer is animating a circle in such a way that the area of the circle increases at a rate of $7\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ How fast is the radius of the circle increasing at the moment when the radius is $1\text{ cm}?$" :question/worked-solution "In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=1,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=7\pi .$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=7\pi $ and $r=1,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}7\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi (1) \\ 7\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =3.5.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the radius is increasing at a rate of $3.5$ centimeters per second."} {:db/id 17592186370594 :question/id #uuid "fe129eff-1d93-5824-989a-6869b87595aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-344789"} {:db/id 17592186395797 :question/id #uuid "a45a10dd-0c29-5839-ade5-5e0193cac871" :question/math-academy-id "q-2870"} {:db/id 17592186506535 :question/id #uuid "37194e35-397f-5f0f-b8ce-0e1f1331cb3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-344726" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7482730a-2ef8-51f5-a35d-2f7208beda4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "45" :db/id 17592186506120}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506120} :answer-field/id #uuid "22d1d24c-d1f3-5b29-bd9f-d25502738b67" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506393}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/1c/1c16496b13f9ad9fc995cc59dedf1777f25e394ca61dd2ea493d8bd8f69c5e14.png)

{{field-1}} ${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{s}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $r$ be the radius of the snowball and let $A$ be its surface area. Both $r$ and $A$ change with time. In particular, we are given that

$$

$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ when $A=100\pi \,{\text{in}}^{2}.$

To start, let's write down the formula for the surface area of a sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 8\pi r\end{aligned}
$$

We then calculate the value of $r$ using $A=100\pi .$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 100\pi  & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 25 & ={r}^{2} \\ r & =\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

Since radius cannot be negative, we have $r=5.$

We now substitute $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{5}$ and $r=5$ into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot 8\pi \cdot 5 \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

What is the radius of the balloon at that moment?" :question/worked-solution "Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =18\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & ={(18\sqrt{\pi })}^{2} \\ A & =324\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

![](images/27/27d0543834333202411a9700401b7e33329a255c7103c9f2ebe394d8c1cf694b.png)

If the radius of the circle is growing, then its area is also increasing. How do we calculate the **rate at which the area is increasing**?

The rate at which the area is changing can be expressed using a derivative:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}
$$

Here, $A$ is the area of the circle, measured in $\textrm{cm}^2,$ and $t$ is the time in seconds. 

We know that the area is related to the radius $r$ as

$$
A = \pi r^2.
$$

Differentiating the above using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r\end{aligned}
$$

Since the radius of a circle is growing at a rate of $2\,\textrm{cm}$ every second, we have $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt} = 2 \, \textrm{cm}.$ Substituting this information, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\cdot 2\pi r=4\pi r\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

And, that's it, we're done! 

If we want to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}$ at a particular moment, we substitute the value of $r$ at that moment into the above. So, for example, if we want to compute $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}$ at the moment when $r=6\,\textrm{cm},$ we plug this into the above and get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 4\pi \cdot 6 = 24\pi\,\textrm{cm}^2/\textrm{s}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6925e269-127a-5cf1-8116-aa809d1cf42f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 488 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2f58c76e-8d14-575a-b5de-62cc2003eb38" :step/math-academy-id Paint dripping onto a floor forms a circular puddle. The radius of the puddle increases at a rate of $10\,\text{in/min}.$ How fast is the area of the puddle increasing at the moment when the radius is $\frac{9}{4\pi }\,\text{in}?$

{{field-1}} ${\text{in}}^{2}\text{/min}.$" :question/worked-solution "In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=\frac{9}{4\pi },$ and we are also told that $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=10.$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=10$ and $r=\frac{9}{4\pi },$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =10\cdot 2\pi (\frac{9}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area of the puddle is increasing at a rate of $45\,{\text{in}}^{2}\text{/min}.$"} :step/id #uuid "f7e7553f-61e4-5efb-b004-ea189584c1c2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186506604}} {:db/id 17592186506650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186369203 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "94f771e8-4826-5b5d-8228-a990eba66454" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\text{ cm}\text{/s}" :db/id 17592186369205} {:answer/id #uuid "75a1d081-eea5-5784-82dd-15b7ad720ca4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.5\text{ cm}\text{/s}" :db/id 17592186369206} {:answer/id #uuid "4f9a3ece-f0fc-5902-8ec9-1de1e79a9224" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\text{ cm}\text{/s}" :db/id 17592186369207} {:answer/id #uuid "fd7b5843-d568-544c-8d66-0fe759b8fdc7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7\text{ cm}\text{/s}" :db/id 17592186369208} {:answer/id #uuid "73d4ba9d-d85b-5d24-b9bf-734a0c435e2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14\text{ cm}\text{/s}" :db/id 17592186369209}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186369206} :answer-field/id #uuid "2882600e-dd6b-59ca-8e2e-a290902aa712" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186369204}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1d90b811-f213-55fb-a391-b4b1340be2c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-116647" :question/problem "![](images/9a/9a864a350b6493794639ea031c7d40242717f5e7325eb326228f82a9cb1c10c9.png)

17592186173097 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173174 :tutorial/content "Recall that the vertex form of a parabola is

$$
y=a(x-h)^2 + k
$$

where $(h,k)$ are the coordinates of the parabola's vertex.

If we are given the equation of a parabola in standard form, we can obtain its vertex form by completing the square.

For example, consider the parabola

$$
y= x^2+6x+16
$$

To express the equation of this parabola in vertex form, we complete the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= x^{2} + 6x + 16 \\
&= x^{2} + 2 \cdot 3 \cdot x + 16 \\
&= x^{2} + 2 \cdot 3 \cdot x + 3^{2} - 3^{2} + 16 \\
&= (x^{2} + 2 \cdot 3 \cdot x + 3^{2}) - 3^{2} + 16 \\
&= (x + 3)^{2} - 3^{2} + 16 \\
&= (x + 3)^{2} - 9 + 16 \\
&= (x + 3)^{2} + 7
\end{aligned}
$$

Expressed in vertex form, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= (x - (-3))^{2} + 7
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex of the parabola is at the point $({\color{blue}-3},{\color{red}7})$." :tutorial/id #uuid "98a78c68-d6fd-5642-a60b-1ac9e65d17ac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5186 :tutorial/title find the algebra in this section a little tricky. It's a good idea to go through it, but you will not be quizzed on it. You may skip this section if you wish.

![](images/2a/2a400b12675f8ebf19ba563192d9ae2296336e40ea380d40e6247564718a2b1f.png)

You may have seen already that for the parabola

$$
y=ax^2+bx+c
$$

with

$$
a\neq 0
$$

the **axis of symmetry** of this parabola is given by the following formula:

$$
x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

We're now in a position to derive this formula.

Since

$$
a \neq 0
$$

we can take out a factor of $a$ from the right-hand side in the parabola formula:

$$
y = a\left(x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + \dfrac{c}{a} \right)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract*

$$
\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2{:}
$$

$$
\underbrace{x^2+{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2}_{\textrm{perfect square}} - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2+ {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

Simplifying the last two terms, we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 - \dfrac{b^2-4ac}{4a^2} = \left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 + \dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a^2}
$$

Next, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a((x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a^{2}}) &= a(x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + a \cdot \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a^{2}} \\
&= a(x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a} \\
&= a(x - (-\frac{b}{2a})_(⏟)_(h))^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a}_(⏟)_(k)
\end{aligned}
$$

By denoting

$$
h=-\dfrac{b}{2a}, \qquad k=\dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a}
$$

we get the equation of the parabola in vertex form:

$$
y = a(x-h)^2 + k
$$

where the vertex is given by

$$
(h,k) = \left(-\dfrac{b}{2a}, \dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a} \right)
$$

Finally, since the parabola's axis of symmetry is the vertical line passing through the vertex, the equation of the axis must be

$$
x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "41e62e06-e589-55dc-846e-1177555ce582" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9116 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Axis of Symmetry Formula"} :step/id #uuid "7ee3f8d6-f452-5eee-97bb-9be3735604ff" :step/math-academy-id 458355}] :activity/title "Writing the Equation of a Parabola in Vertex Form" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172214} {:db/id 17592186173097 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173174 :tutorial/content "Recall that the vertex form of a parabola is

y=ax^2+bx+c
$$

with

$$
a\neq 0
$$

the **axis of symmetry** of this parabola is given by the following formula:

$$
x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

We're now in a position to derive this formula.

Since

$$
a \neq 0
$$

we can take out a factor of $a$ from the right-hand side in the parabola formula:

$$
y = a\left(x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + \dfrac{c}{a} \right)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract*

$$
\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2{:}
$$

$$
\underbrace{x^2+{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2}_{\textrm{perfect square}} - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2+ {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

Simplifying the last two terms, we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 - \dfrac{b^2-4ac}{4a^2} = \left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 + \dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a^2}
$$

Next, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a((x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a^{2}}) &= a(x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + a \cdot \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a^{2}} \\
&= a(x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a} \\
&= a(x - (-\frac{b}{2a})_(⏟)_(h))^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a}_(⏟)_(k)
\end{aligned}
$$

By denoting

$$
h=-\dfrac{b}{2a}, \qquad k=\dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a}
$$

we get the equation of the parabola in vertex form:

$$
y = a(x-h)^2 + k
$$

where the vertex is given by

$$
(h,k) = \left(-\dfrac{b}{2a}, \dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a} \right)
$$

Finally, since the parabola's axis of symmetry is the vertical line passing through the vertex, the equation of the axis must be

$$
x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "41e62e06-e589-55dc-846e-1177555ce582" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9116 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Axis of Symmetry Formula"} {:db/id 17592186049503 :topic/difficulty 0.6614631241392411 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428889 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$" :question/worked-solution "If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

17592186163031 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163306 :tutorial/content "The invertible matrix theorem tells us that if $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix with full rank (i.e., $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$), then there exists a unique inverse matrix $A^{-1}$ such that 

$$
AA^{-1}=A^{-1}\!A=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ denotes the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

There are two questions that we can ask:

- Can we extend the notion of an inverse matrix to one that works for $n\times n$ matrices $A$ where $\mathrm{rank}(A) < n?$

- Is it possible to generalize the concept of an inverse to non-square matrices?

The answer to both questions is yes! This generalization of the inverse of $A$ is called the **pseudoinverse** of $A,$ and is denoted $A^+.$ The dimensions of $A^+$ are the same as $A^T.$

As an example, let's consider the ${\color{red}{3}}\times {\color{blue}{2}}$ matrix $A$ and its corresponding pseudoinverse, given below:

![](images/87/87581a69d3d76dbf3b0ebca8941c9a82b5b9443b00e86f32e4e9e4a42ef5e18b.svg)

- Computing $A^{+}\!A,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+}\,A & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

which is the identity matrix $I_{\color{blue}{2}}.$

- Computing $A\!A^{+},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{+} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which is *almost* the identity matrix $I_{\color{red}{3}}.$

We can explain this result using the following properties of the pseudoinverse:

- *If the columns of an $m\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $A^+A = I_{\color{blue}{n}}.$*

- *If the rows of an ${\color{red}{m}}\times n$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $AA^+ = I_{\color{red}{m}}.$*

In the example above, the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, but the rows are not.

Moreover, the notion of a pseudoinverse is consistent with inverse matrices. In particular,

*If $A$ is an invertible square matrix, then $A^{+} = A^{-1}.$*

![](images/98/987aa533ca51a9f101ba590b7ade0753983ae219534342aad42054316b2e02ec.svg)

and its singular value decomposition $A=U \Sigma V ^T,$ where

![](images/69/69e68ac94c6e25b2609f7d20616d7d564a1225abad748c3e4fd94516cb6df72f.svg)

Notice that $\Sigma$ contains a row of zeros. In these situations, it's possible to simplify the decomposition of $A.$ This simplified decomposition is called the **reduced singular value decomposition** of $A.$

First, we note that $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix. In addition, the matrix $\Sigma$ has two non-zero singular values on its main diagonal, so the rank of $A$ is $\color{blue}r=2.$ 

To find our reduced SVD, we proceed as follows:

- First, we remove all zero rows and columns from $\Sigma.$ In our example, we should delete the $3$rd row since it contains only zeros. Notice that we obtain a square invertible matrix of rank ${\color{blue}2}{:}$ 
![](images/a5/a56440b8808003f25bec4b61d4d06af7274a5eea68da4e94af9e91af8d64d02a.svg)

- Next, we remove all extra columns of $U$ starting from the right, keeping only $\color{blue}2$ columns. In our example, we should delete the $3$rd column:
![](images/e4/e4ba93ef3588affc421af821cb9de1051749396c69a9e64523399f7fc4e3bc5b.svg)

- Finally, we remove all extra columns of $V$ starting from the right, keeping only $\color{blue}2$ columns. In our example, we should keep $V$ as it is since it already has only $2$ columns: 
![](images/b1/b146b37075dda593ded5b86d58e6cfba3de463e01727b39756a6b90cbb88a95f.svg)

The reduced singular value decomposition of $A$ is then given by

$$
A = U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T.
$$

So, in our example, we have

![](images/c1/c1eed35f9b7aa3214e9783f8f80952e57adca6c4d4b81efaeb49255b5973f3af.svg)

In general, a singular value decomposition 

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T
$$

 

of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is not unique. However, we can always simplify it to the corresponding reduced singular value decomposition 

$$
A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T
$$

 

with the following properties:

- $\Sigma_r$ is a square diagonal matrix of size $r\times r,$ where $r\leq \min\{m,n\}$ is the rank of $A.$ The main diagonal of $\Sigma_r$ contains the non-zero singular values $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_r$ of $A$ in descending order.

- $U_r$ is a $m\times r$ matrix obtained by keeping only the first $r$ columns of $U.$

- $V_r$ is a $n \times r$ matrix obtained by keeping only the first $r$ columns of $V.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "924b4229-0b49-5d81-9255-b9be0ec07ab6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6075 :tutorial/title "Reduced Singular Value Decomposition"} :step/id #uuid "0c540186-c349-53ef-8094-366eb44f526a" :step/math-academy-id 36969 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163035}} {:db/id 17592186163035 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162091 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161904 :question/id #uuid "66c34c76-6243-50b8-832f-027abb6ab736" :question/math-academy-id "e-9830"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ff858037-da99-53e9-acdc-e4963e7d765e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162348} {:db/id 17592186162359} {:db/id 17592186371810} {:db/id 17592186383389} {:db/id 17592186383396} {:db/id 17592186388552} {:db/id 17592186388559} {:db/id 17592186388566} {:db/id 17592186420790} {:db/id 17592186420791} {:db/id 17592186420792} {:db/id 17592186511568}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Reduced Singular Value Decomposition"} :step/id #uuid "03964208-b7f5-5c5d-ab41-385b66f7efbd" :step/math-academy-id 36970 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163039}} {:db/id 17592186163039 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163309 :tutorial/content "Recall that the least-squares solution of the system 

$$
A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b},
$$

is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that $\| A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|$ is minimized. 

The least-squares solution is not unique when $A$ has linearly dependent columns. However, it can be shown that a so-called **optimal least-squares solution** $\mathbf{x^\ast}$ always exists. The optimal least-squares solution is the solution to the least squares problem with the shortest possible length.

It turns out that the optimal least-squares solution can be found using the pseudoinverse of $A,$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf{x^\ast} = A^{+} \mathbf{b}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6f731acb-e452-5433-88a5-1e2c66fd5a84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6078 :tutorial/title "The Optimal Least-Squares Solution"} :step/id #uuid "f03c737f-a30a-5ef1-8ade-d5c1bd49e933" :step/math-academy-id 36979} {:db/id 17592186163046 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163313 :tutorial/content "There are many ways to find the pseudoinverse of a given matrix $A.$ One way is to use the singular value decomposition of $A{:}$

Specifically, if 

$$
A=U \Sigma V ^T
$$

is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
A^+ = V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T,
$$

 
where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bd110f79-cfe0-58f8-b7e6-ea9baa7814d9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6102 :tutorial/title "Finding the Pseudoinverse Using Singular Value Decomposition"} :step/id #uuid "cef3aa4e-1b1d-50ea-b285-5cc2dcac6f73" :step/math-academy-id 37091 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163032}} {:db/id 17592186163047 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163314 :tutorial/content "For an *almost* zero ${\color{red}{m}}\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
\sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r
$$

on the main diagonal only, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the *almost* zero ${\color{blue}{n}}\times {\color{red}{m}}$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}
$$

on the main diagonal only.

For example, for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/d6/d6d6a167747f99c5a48be59ae3e11ca7b5a9188e80ddeb63b8c0f193d991b18c.svg)

we calculate its pseudoinverse as follows:

- **Step 1:** Replace the non-zero elements on the main diagonal with their multiplicative inverses.

- **Step 2:** Transpose the resulting matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}}^{+} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{3}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {4}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1/3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8709222e-61fc-512e-82ff-3564c1513100" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6103 :tutorial/title "The Pseudoinverse of an Almost Diagonal Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "e5289df4-d145-54b7-a6f3-e8e13a522ee7" :step/math-academy-id 37092 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163033}}] :activity/title "Singular Value Decomposition and the Pseudoinverse Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162228} {:db/id 17592186163031 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163306 :tutorial/content "The invertible matrix theorem tells us that if $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix with full rank (i.e., $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$), then there exists a unique inverse matrix $A^{-1}$ such that 

$$
AA^{-1}=A^{-1}\!A=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ denotes the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

There are two questions that we can ask:

- Can we extend the notion of an inverse matrix to one that works for $n\times n$ matrices $A$ where $\mathrm{rank}(A) < n?$

- Is it possible to generalize the concept of an inverse to non-square matrices?

The answer to both questions is yes! This generalization of the inverse of $A$ is called the **pseudoinverse** of $A,$ and is denoted $A^+.$ The dimensions of $A^+$ are the same as $A^T.$

As an example, let's consider the ${\color{red}{3}}\times {\color{blue}{2}}$ matrix $A$ and its corresponding pseudoinverse, given below:

![](images/87/87581a69d3d76dbf3b0ebca8941c9a82b5b9443b00e86f32e4e9e4a42ef5e18b.svg)

- Computing $A^{+}\!A,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+}\,A & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

which is the identity matrix $I_{\color{blue}{2}}.$

- Computing $A\!A^{+},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{+} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which is *almost* the identity matrix $I_{\color{red}{3}}.$

We can explain this result using the following properties of the pseudoinverse:

- *If the columns of an $m\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $A^+A = I_{\color{blue}{n}}.$*

- *If the rows of an ${\color{red}{m}}\times n$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $AA^+ = I_{\color{red}{m}}.$*

In the example above, the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, but the rows are not.

Moreover, the notion of a pseudoinverse is consistent with inverse matrices. In particular,

*If $A$ is an invertible square matrix, then $A^{+} = A^{-1}.$*

This lesson will discuss how to compute the pseudoinverse for any matrix, starting with an important special case." :tutorial/id #uuid "6cec9ecf-529c-566f-9895-3fde09f24253" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6074 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a081b9a8-d058-5b79-8d8b-a8471a1f524a" :step/math-academy-id 36962 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163047}} {:db/id 17592186163306 :tutorial/content "The invertible matrix theorem tells us that if $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix with full rank (i.e., $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$), then there exists a unique inverse matrix $A^{-1}$ such that

In general, a singular value decomposition 

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T
$$

 

of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is not unique. However, we can always simplify it to the corresponding reduced singular value decomposition 

$$
A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T
$$

 

with the following properties:

- $\Sigma_r$ is a square diagonal matrix of size $r\times r,$ where $r\leq \min\{m,n\}$ is the rank of $A.$ The main diagonal of $\Sigma_r$ contains the non-zero singular values $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_r$ of $A$ in descending order.

- $U_r$ is a $m\times r$ matrix obtained by keeping only the first $r$ columns of $U.$

denominator works similarly for algebraic expressions as it does for numerical ones. When the denominator contains two terms and includes radicals, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the *conjugate* of the denominator to eliminate the radical.

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}}
$$

To find the conjugate of the denominator $1+\sqrt{x}$, all we have to do is flip the sign between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is

$$
1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{x}
$$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by $1-\sqrt{x}$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}} &=  \\
\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}} \cdot \frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - \sqrt{x}} &=  \\
(1 - \sqrt{x})/((1 + \sqrt{x})(1 - \sqrt{x})) &=  \\
(1 - \sqrt{x})/(1^{2} - (\sqrt{x})^{2}) &=  \\
&= \frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - x}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8dde46d5-669e-5c3a-b471-7541b1824862" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13464 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7c88995e-61d0-5dad-a452-dff7902b363d" 17592186213279} {:db/id 17592186213857 :step/content {:db/id 17592186214235 :tutorial/content "Rationalizing the denominator works similarly for algebraic expressions as it does for numerical ones. When the denominator contains two terms and includes radicals, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the *conjugate* of the denominator to eliminate the radical.

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}}
$$

To find the conjugate of the denominator $1+\sqrt{x}$, all we have to do is flip the sign between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is

$$
1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{x}
$$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by $1-\sqrt{x}$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}} &=  \\
\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}} \cdot \frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - \sqrt{x}} &=  \\
(1 - \sqrt{x})/((1 + \sqrt{x})(1 - \sqrt{x})) &=  \\
(1 - \sqrt{x})/(1^{2} - (\sqrt{x})^{2}) &=  \\
&= \frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - x}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8dde46d5-669e-5c3a-b471-7541b1824862" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13464 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7c88995e-61d0-5dad-a452-dff7902b363d" :step/math-academy-id 478497 :step/next {:db/id 17592186213858}} {:db/id 17592186214235 :tutorial/content "Rationalizing the denominator works similarly for algebraic expressions as it does for numerical ones. We get

$$
\begin{aligned} \cos\theta & = 0.64\ \arccos(\cos\theta) & = \arccos(0.64) \ \theta&=\arccos(0.64) \end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha & = 1.25 \ \arctan(\tan\alpha) & =\arctan(1.25) \ \alpha&=\arctan(1.25). \end{aligned}
$$

Then, using a calculator, we find

$$
\begin{aligned} \theta + \alpha & =\arccos(0.64)+\arctan(1.25) \\ &=(50.208...)^{\circ} + (51.340...)^{\circ} \\ & = (101.548...)^{\circ} \\ & \approx 102^{\circ} \end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

**Watch out!** If we round $\theta$ and $\alpha$ to the nearest integer, we get

$$
\theta \approx 50^\circ
$$

and

$$
\alpha \approx 51^\circ
$$

After we sum up the angles we get an incorrect result:

$$
θ + α \mid \approx 50^{∘} + 51^{∘} = 101^{∘}
$$

The correct answer is $102^\circ$, not $101^\circ$. This is a rounding error! To avoid this kind of error we have to round *after* we take the sum, not before."} {:db/id 17592186078842 :question/id #uuid "664d5698-098c-5a14-b9f6-7c7cc0d472f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-27925"} {:db/id 17592186078843 :question/id #uuid "e3f75d09-f893-53bd-8c12-a90fcd54f324" :question/math-academy-id "q-27926"} {:db/id 17592186078397 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078261 :question/id #uuid "7a4aa28f-8a0b-556f-b6ce-beb674cd0234" :question/math-academy-id "e-3253"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8ccd79e-56a6-58fc-917c-8dc660ad2425" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049915}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078738 :question/id #uuid "767498d7-19f9-5d8e-b746-de5fdc918b99" :question/math-academy-id "q-14640"} {:db/id 17592186078739 :question/id #uuid "12b5b733-b14d-5f7f-ba68-052336cddf60" :question/math-academy-id "q-14642"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Measure of an Angle Given the Lengths of Two Sides of a Right Triangle"} {:db/id 17592186078261 :question/id #uuid "7a4aa28f-8a0b-556f-b6ce-beb674cd0234" :question/math-academy-id "e-3253" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186078397 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8ccd79e-56a6-58fc-917c-8dc660ad2425" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Measure of an Angle Given the Lengths of Two Sides of a Right Triangle"}] :question/problem "In a right triangle $\triangle ABC$, we have $AC = 9$, $BC=13$, and $m\angle A = \alpha$. Given that $\overline{AB}$ is the hypotenuse of the triangle, find the value of $\alpha$ (rounded to one decimal place)." :question/worked-solution "Let's sketch the triangle that's described.

![](images/29/29ab71a468b9a57842e07ef74b8d8d770c7ebfacabb3735694c0dd40303ad220.png)

Since we are given the lengths of the adjacent and opposite sides, we can use tangent to find the angle measurement. We have

$$
\tan \alpha= \dfrac{\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{adjacent}} = \dfrac{13}{9}
$$

We now calculate $\alpha$ using the inverse tangent:

$$
\begin{aligned} \tan \alpha &= \dfrac{13}{9} \\[5pt] \arctan(\tan \alpha) &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{13}{9} \right) \\[5pt] \alpha &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{13}{9} \right) \\[5pt] &=(55.304\,8...)^\circ \\[5pt] &\approx 55.3^\circ \end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place."} {:db/id 17592186049915} {:db/id 17592186078738 :question/id #uuid "767498d7-19f9-5d8e-b746-de5fdc918b99" :question/math-academy-id "q-14640"} {:db/id 17592186078739 :tutorial/content "Using a calculator, we can evaluate sine for the angle of $20^\circ$, and get

$$
\sin(20^{\circ}) \approx 0.342
$$

But what if we are given the value $0.342$, and we want to find the angle whose sine is this value? To do this, we can use the **inverse trigonometric functions**.

In the case of the sine, its inverse is **arcsine** (written as $\arcsin$ or $\sin^{-1}$). If applied to the sine, it gives the value of the angle:

$$
\arcsin (0.342) \approx 20^{\circ}
$$

The inverses of the other trigonometric functions work in the same way.

- The inverse of sine is $\arcsin$.
- The inverse of cosine is $\arccos$.
- The inverse of tangent is $\arctan$.

Try it for yourself. But make sure that your calculator is in "degrees" mode!

**Note:** In this topic, we only deal with acute angles. Things get a little more complicated for non-acute angles, but you'll learn about that later!" :tutorial/id #uuid "259189af-6378-518d-a123-d831688aed97" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2450 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f93cf90c-35eb-5ffe-884d-35a89ebf6a8b" :step/math-academy-id 10975 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079247}} {:db/id 17592186079247 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078395 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078259 :question/id #uuid "200cec1b-b266-557f-a2ef-db02cf6d941a" :question/math-academy-id "e-3251"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8e4cc25e-b0e9-5935-86f7-c450c990cef8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048438}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078840} {:db/id 17592186078841}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Value of an Inverse Trigonometric Ratio"} :step/id #uuid "148b95eb-c3f7-5f1b-881e-5dc27b007df7" :step/math-academy-id 10976 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079259}} {:db/id 17592186079248 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078396 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078260 :question/id #uuid "01ba80ea-e3d7-5372-9732-d721f039bae8" :question/math-academy-id "e-3252"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "81772ee2-6b04-559c-85a3-976fd12bbd74" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050867}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078842} {:db/id 17592186078843}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Unknown Angles Using Inverse Trigonometric Functions"} :step/id #uuid "9ac21fb4-7047-5b4d-879f-08f183f19294" :step/math-academy-id 10977 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079249}} {:db/id 17592186079249 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079641 :tutorial/content "The inverse trigonometric functions are particularly useful when we need to find the measure of an angle in a right triangle.

To demonstrate, let's find the measure of the angle $\theta$ indicated in the triangle below.

![](images/85/85c384f5cbfc9d9bfa4ffebeafc3dbe66eb756e71f4790b0d9566ebdab559f9c.png)

Since we are given the length of the hypotenuse and opposite sides to $\theta$, we can use sine to find the angle measurement. We have

$$
\begin{aligned} \sin (\theta) = \dfrac{\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} &= \dfrac{5}{7}. \end{aligned}
$$

We now calculate $\theta$ using the inverse sine:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sin (\theta) &= \dfrac{5}{7} \\[5pt] \arcsin(\sin (\theta)) &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{5}{7} \right) \\[5pt] \theta &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{5}{7} \right) \\[5pt] &=(45.584\,6...)^\circ \\[5pt] &\approx 46^\circ \end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a55899c-f08a-5577-a1de-9fb483947ddf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2451 :tutorial/title "Finding the Measure of an Angle in a Right Triangle Using Trigonometry"} :step/id #uuid "ffeda555-fc7d-5cb3-ba37-a29037e0cba3" :step/math-academy-id 10978 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079250}} {:db/id 17592186079250 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078397 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078261 :question/id #uuid "7a4aa28f-8a0b-556f-b6ce-beb674cd0234" :question/math-academy-id "e-3253"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8ccd79e-56a6-58fc-917c-8dc660ad2425" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049915}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078738} {:db/id 17592186078739}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Measure of an Angle Given the Lengths of Two Sides of a Right Triangle"} :step/id #uuid "1b2e5432-c30a-5106-99bc-487755ce72bf" :step/math-academy-id 10979} {:db/id 17592186079259 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079648 :tutorial/content "If we have a trigonometric equation like

$$
\cos \theta = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

and we want to solve for $\theta$, we can apply the corresponding inverse trigonometric function to both sides of the equation to "cancel" out the trigonometric function.

Here, the trigonometric function is $\cos$, so the inverse trigonometric function is $\arccos$, and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\arccos (\cos θ) &= \arccos (\frac{1}{2}) \\
θ &= 60^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9953e2ac-f857-5760-a8b2-c5c56367a048" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2560 :tutorial/title "Applying an Inverse Trigonometric Function to Both Sides of an Equation"} :step/id #uuid "bd5b2322-661e-5aa8-9d7a-05b0dd05892e" :step/math-academy-id 11738 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079248}}] :activity/title "Calculating Angles in Right Triangles Using Trigonometry" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186078640} {:db/id 17592186079246 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079640 :tutorial/content "Using a calculator, we can evaluate sine for the angle of $20^\circ$, and get

![](images/85/85c384f5cbfc9d9bfa4ffebeafc3dbe66eb756e71f4790b0d9566ebdab559f9c.png)

Since we are given the length of the hypotenuse and opposite sides to $\theta$, we can use sine to find the angle measurement. We have

$$
\begin{aligned} \sin (\theta) = \dfrac{\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} &= \dfrac{5}{7}. \end{aligned}
$$

We now calculate $\theta$ using the inverse sine:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sin (\theta) &= \dfrac{5}{7} \\[5pt] \arcsin(\sin (\theta)) &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{5}{7} \right) \\[5pt] \theta &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{5}{7} \right) \\[5pt] &=(45.584\,6...)^\circ \\[5pt] &\approx 46^\circ \end{aligned}
$$

Rates"}] :question/problem "A $6\,\text{m}$ tall street lamp is casting a shadow of a $1.5\,\text{m}$ woman onto the ground.
